6

The contemporary ultrarich aren’t as interesting for our purposes because they mostly either work or socialize extensively with people who do. The 1980s might have been the last decade when wealthy women were free of the expectation to have some kind of job. I’ve heard that this might be different for Gulf citizen men, but I’m still looking for good ethnographic literature on them.

7

Herbert J. Gans, The Urban Villagers: Group and Class in the Life of Italian-Americans (The Free Press of Glencoe, 1962).

8

While I will focus on Gans here, Young and Willmott and Coing made broadly similar arguments about their own subjects.

9

Claudia Strauss, What Work Means: Beyond the Puritan Work Ethic (Cornell University Press, 2024), 236–37.

10

An accountant in the 1970s needed a high school diploma and the ability to convincingly claim they liked math.

11

See Allan Silver, “Friendship in Commercial Society: Eighteenth-Century Social Theory and Modern Sociology,” American Journal of Sociology 95, no. 6 (1990): 1474–1504.

item.title: Behind the scenes: After Work, We’ll Have Each Other
item.description: Asterisk editor in chief Clara Collier on what everyone is getting wrong about “AI and work.”
item.content:encoded:
By Angela Chen

In this behind-the-scenes interview, Asterisk managing editor Angela Chen interviews editor in chief Clara Collier about her essay After Work, We’ll Have Each Other. The two discuss why meaning is such a slippery concept, why European salon culture was not an intellectual paradise, and why we should fear the relational world.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Angela Chen: The original version of your essay began with this long intro referring to certain conversations you’d been having about “AI and work.” I made you cut that intro because we needed this essay to be a reasonable length, but I promised you we’d talk about why you found those discussion so frustrating.

Clara Collier: There’s so much I cut — I think I cut more than made it into the final piece. And I should say, a lot of these conversations were with people I deeply respect, who have important thoughts. It’s not that everyone talking about the future of work is wrong. But I was having a lot of conversations in circles where there’s a fairly common belief that human labor will be obviated one way or another. I’m on the fence about this myself, but I think it’s an important issue to think through.

Anyway, a common answer was, “We’ll get our meaning from personal relationships.” My response was that this is how the vast majority of cultures have worked throughout history, and it wasn’t better, it was worse!

Angela: Before we get to why it was worse, I’m still thinking about how there was a whole tangent about “meaning” that you eventually cut because it was too broad and too slippery. Can you tell me about the reading and thinking you did when you thought the piece would focus more on that?

Clara: I read Viktor Frankl — Man’s Search for Meaning — and went down a whole tangent through the meaning of “meaning” in mid-century thought. Maslow is the big one — most people know him as “the pyramid guy,” but he also wrote a book called Eupsychian Management, about how to run a business in a way that’s psychologically wholesome for employees. That book helped popularize the idea — he wasn’t the first to say it, but he helped establish — that a good management environment is one where an employee’s identity is wrapped up in their work, and the work helps them become a fuller person. Douglas McGregor, working alongside him, popularized a lot of this too.

The reason I was reading all this — and also the reason it ended up getting cut — is that I think “meaning” is a very slippery term. When someone says they lack meaning in their life, that can usually be broken down into something more concrete. Often it means they’re lonely, or that they lack a sense of accomplishment. That can be broken down further — sometimes it means they feel their work isn’t sufficiently respected by their peers, sometimes it means they don’t feel useful, sometimes it means they’re not living up to an assigned social role, like being a provider.

The idea of “work as a source of meaning” implies there’s a single, interchangeable thing called meaning — that if you’re not getting it from your job, you can get it from something else. I don’t think that’s how this cluster of psychological needs actually works, at least in modern American society. Many men with rich, fulfilling family lives but who are unemployed would still feel a lack of meaning, because it’s culturally significant for them to be able to provide. And there are plenty of people with good jobs they find useful and meaningful who are still unhappy because they don’t have a romantic partner.

Angela: In the essay, what you arrive at is that you’re not really talking about meaning. You’re talking about dignity.

Clara: I want to explain why I think this is more than a semantic distinction. The idea that work specifically is a source of meaning is a very modern one. That’s why I was reading 1950s organizational psychologists, and also why I was reading about the history of the American work ethic in the 19th century. So whenever someone asks, “What will we do without work as a source of meaning?” — the answer is: probably the same things almost every human society before about 1800 did, because that concept simply didn’t exist for them.

Angela: This essay was compelling to me because one of the arguments is that we already know what a world without work looks like, even though people often claim that we don’t. Why is it so hard for people to reach for those historical examples?

Clara: It depends who we’re talking about. A lot of post-work philosophers come out of a socialist tradition, so they’re not looking to the past — it’s more deeply ingrained in their worldview that there will be a transformative change in human economic relations that creates something incommensurable with what came before. I disagree with that, but I understand the motivation.

People coming at this more from an “AI will obviate all work” angle tend to be less interested in history, or less familiar with it, or don’t see it as relevant.

I also hear the argument that so much will change about the material conditions of society that anything from the past is a bad analogy. That’s coherent, but I still think historical precedent is better than flying blind, and that these relational patterns have persisted across enormous technological changes throughout human history. I don’t think there’s nothing to learn from patterns that recur across wildly different societies and contexts.

Angela: Yeah. We’re still just apes. We’re still chimpanzees, in a way, with the same drives around belonging and status.

Clara: Right — that goes back to what I was saying before I got sidetracked. This whole essay has been an exercise in tangent-taming.

The reason I think dignity and meaning are meaningfully distinct is that meaning is a fuzzy phrase that collapses into a lot of different things. The idea that meaning in the sense of personal self-fulfillment comes from work, or even that it matters at all, is pretty contingent.. What isn’t historically contingent — what every human culture has valued — is having an understanding of what you have to do to be a successful, functioning member of your society and to earn the respect of your peers.

Angela: Is that about status? Is that the word we’re dancing around?

Clara: I actually thought about using the word status for this and decided not to because status is positional, and I don’t think dignity is necessarily positional. Status would be things like: do you have the best job, the biggest house, the most attractive spouse, the most money, the highest-achieving kids?

But there are many paths to dignity in our society that don’t require winning on any of those axes. Some important determinants of dignity in modern American society are things like having a steady job, owning a house, being married, being a parent. Not that you need all of these to be dignified — but if you asked a random parent whether their child had a successful life, those are the boxes they’d check.

I don’t think that’s universal — there are plenty of societies where dignity and status are much more closely tied, and dignity is much more positional. Our society, compared to the broad sweep of human cultures — at least post-agriculture — is actually fairly egalitarian on this front.

Visions from the relational world

Angela: So, the “meaning” material collapsed into too many things and you set it aside in favor of the relational material. For that, most of the piece is really built on the ethnographies you were reading. Walk me through how you chose which ones. I know you started with court memoirs.

Clara: That’s right — I knew from the beginning that the memoirs of the Duc de Saint-Simon would be the starting point. If we’re thinking about a post-work society, aristocracies are a natural place to look. They’re vast and varied — military aristocracies, governing aristocracies — but broadly, there are plenty of historical examples of societies where people are mostly wealthy, and to the extent they’re not, they don’t meet their material needs through productive labor.

They meet them by managing their network of social relationships, and they actively disdain the idea of paid work. But they still do things. So why do they do what they do? How do they spend their time? That felt directly relevant to a world where our material needs are mostly met, and to the extent they’re not, we meet them by leveraging our social networks.

Angela: Then we had this whole discussion about salons, and how people are like, “we’ll just all be talking to Voltaire all the time.” But it seems like that wasn’t the case.

Clara: This is a contested area. The historian Antoine Lilti is responding to earlier historians who wrote about the importance of salon culture. What Lilti argues is that the ideal of the salon is largely fictional — based mostly on accounts written after the French Revolution by people romanticizing a culture that no longer existed.

The accounts are not contemporaneous — but we do have a lot of contemporaneous material: memoirs, letters. When you look at what these conversations actually consisted of, there wasn’t much high-minded philosophical discussion. Voltaire and Diderot really were invited to these gatherings, and they were influential spaces. But that doesn’t mean the salons were primarily about expanding the aristocrats’ minds. It was more of a status marker. The actual bulk of the conversation was political gossip — people talking about themselves.

This is a pattern you see again and again: bourgeois people copying elements of aristocratic culture, but with a much rosier view of it, so they end up far more invested in performing intellectualism — which wasn’t really something true aristocrats typically care about. Of course there are exceptions, but it’s not the norm.

Angela: The next book you cover is Susan Ostrander’s Women of the Upper Class, from 1984. Did you know going in you’d use this book, or did you find it along the way?

Clara:. One thing I struggled with throughout is that there are countless case studies I could have used. It was hard to narrow down. But I felt that the strongest counterargument to using the aristocratic memoirs is that it’s a very particular world — not just that they don’t work, but that they’re living under a kind of enlightened absolutism, with particular economic, social, and political conditions which aren’t even typical of most aristocracies, let alone anything that exists today. If we simply removed work from our modern American lives, the situation would look very different. So I wanted to find something that asked: what if we removed work specifically from modern American lives? That’s how I found Ostrander.

Total American cultural victory

Angela: We’re both independently reading various ethnographies, and it turns out ours cite each other. I didn’t read Ostrander, but I read Uneasy Street, which is fieldwork from 2009ish on rich New Yorkers. One of the biggest differences is how concerned these New Yorkers are with staying proximate to work. If they’re not working, they’ll talk about how they used to, or frame something like running the household as labor, even though it’s uncompensated. That’s not something you see in Ostrander at all.

Clara: Not at all. And it’s more than just New York. I was talking with a friend who’s a philanthropic consultant for very wealthy clients, and she told me that among the global ultra-rich today, everyone wants either a vanity job or to emphasize that something like motherhood is real work — which is, frankly, a total American cultural victory. De Tocqueville wrote about this back in 1831! Rich Americans are unlike rich Europeans in that they’re really, really anxious about the idea of being idle. They all have this compulsion to do something work-like. But of course he’s talking about men.

Angela: What do you make of the shift between 1985 and 2009?

Clara: I think several things are happening. Partly it’s the social changes of the ‘60s still working their way through American society — the women’s movement especially. In Ostrander’s sample, the women aren’t really in a work-free society in a deep sense — their husbands all work, some of them manage the family money but still go into an office to do it, while the women, with just one exception, don’t work at all. They grew up in an America where women not working was completely normal and not seen as something to overcome.

By the time you reach the younger women in that sample, some say things like, “I kind of regret not having a paid job” — they won’t frame what they’re doing as proximate to work. Those women mark the end of a generation where women not working was totally socially unmarked in America. So this anxiety about not working has always existed in the American upper classes, but now it’s spread to the women.

Angela: And in Uneasy Street, nobody likes talking about money — people are embarrassed by how much they have and don’t want to disclose it. Was money discussed openly in Ostrander’s book?

Clara: No dollar amounts are mentioned, but there isn’t the same sense of embarrassment — I think because this is a culture with a still-intact sense of noblesse oblige. This is actually another thing I think the women’s movement changed.

Ostrander’s central argument is that the women’s volunteering and socializing was fulfilling an important role in legitimizing their wealth and status — constructing a sense that it’s good and normal that they have these advantages, because they fulfill an important role in the community. As more women entered paid work, they stopped fulfilling that legitimating function. This isn’t necessarily about whether other people see their wealth as legitimate, it’s how people of this class think about themselves.

In a way, the past few decades have proven Ostrander’s thesis — once women stopped doing that legitimating work, it fundamentally changed how that entire class relates to and justifies its position.

Angela: Ostrander’s book is set in Cleveland, while Uneasy Street is very New York — the Hamptons, Groton. What differences do you see between New York and Bay Area wealth?

Clara: It’s very different — in SF, almost none of the wealth is inherited, and there’s been much less time for these justifying mechanisms to develop. Even the “old money” in Ostrander’s book isn’t that old in objective terms — a few generations, maybe a hundred years — so these aren’t defenses passed down from time immemorial. It’s a set of behaviors and justifications that accreted as circumstances arose.

People in SF, I think, feel less need to justify wealth generally, but there’s a very strong philanthropic drive. I think that comes less from a need to justify being wealthy and more from an extension of having goals in the world and wanting to apply resources toward them.

Angela: One reason you wrote about this was to push back on the idea that if none of us had to work for money, we’d all just become painters — and instead you show these women doing volunteer busy-work, not painting. I’m curious: in SF specifically, it does seem like a lot of people have side projects alongside their day jobs. Is there a sense that, for this particular group, the “painter” outcome might actually hold true — even if it doesn’t generalize?

Clara: I’ve had many conversations about this. There are definitely people for whom it’s true — if they didn’t have to work, they’d pursue their passion projects. I think they’re overrepresented in this conversation, which leads them to misjudge how most people would actually react to that situation. We have plenty of examples — not just among wealthy people, but across the economic spectrum — of people who don’t handle unstructured freedom well.

The Gulf states are a good example, and some Pacific Islands that had mineral discoveries — places where, because of some natural windfall, citizens don’t have to work, and governments end up inventing busy-work jobs for them. I think self-actualization is genuinely difficult, and one thing I’ve come to believe fairly strongly from this reading is that we don’t have great tools for encouraging self-actualization at a societal level.

Broadly distributed material prosperity certainly makes things easier to follow your dreams, but even among the rich, wanting to orient your life around some inner passion is quite rare. I don’t think we’ve ever figured out how to get more than a tiny minority of people to even want to self-actualize in this way, and I don’t think it’s a very useful goal for social planning.

Angela: Later in the essay, you quote Claudia Strauss and discuss surveys and ethnographies about how people actually feel about work, even work they don’t love. Did anything in that research surprise you?

Clara: I should say up front — I know I’m lucky in my own job. It’s intellectually engaging, not too physically demanding, and I have a lot of autonomy. In many ways it’s a classically “good” job, and I understand that not all jobs are good — many are genuinely miserable, and plenty of people would be individually happier without their particular job.

That said, I talk to a lot of people in my position who assume the world is divided into people with good jobs and people who are miserable. That’s not the case. Survey and ethnographic evidence is fairly consistent, at least here in the U.S.: most Americans like working — even people in classically boring jobs generally prefer going to work over not going. That’s an important thing to understand about how people would actually react to not having to work.

I do want to add some balance here. I truly believe that the Court of Versailles was dystopian for everyone involved. But most relational groups aren’t dystopian. I don’t think it’s simply a terrible way to live. But I do think that way of living is deeply limiting, with real costs — especially for people who don’t fit that mold well.

item.title: We need an AI adverse event reporting system
item.description: Clara Collier interviews Jessica Dai.
item.content:encoded:
By Clara Collier

ChatGPT was released on November 30, 2022; the subreddit r/ChatGPT was created just one day later. In a recent paper, Jessica Dai, a PhD candidate in computer science at UC Berkeley, and her coauthors analyze three years of posts from r/ChatGPT to understand how users’ experiences with ChatGPT have changed over time.

They used unsupervised machine-learning methods to surface recurring themes in ~137,000 posts, then tracked how those themes rise and fall alongside major product and model releases. The paper also introduces a method for doing this kind of analysis prospectively: continually updating its picture of what users are talking about and statistically flagging meaningful changes as they emerge.

Asterisk editor in chief Clara Collier interviews Jessica about the findings, AI incidents, and building a better system.

This interview has been edited for clarity.

Clara Collier: Hi, Jessica. Do you want to start by telling me a little bit about your new paper? What would be most surprising to me, as someone in tech circles who checks r/ChatGPT and related subreddits but doesn’t follow them closely?

Jessica: One thing I think you can only really see in a quantitative study of this scale is the change in how people post about using ChatGPT for things we call emotional engagement. This would be therapy use cases, emotional support, companionship, romantic relationships, and so on.

People have been posting about those things since the very beginning. But something you can see when you look at all the data over time is that really soon after the release of GPT-4o — this is in May 2024 — the frequency at which people post about these topics starts increasing almost immediately. I don’t want to make super strong causal claims here, because the memory feature was a couple of weeks before that, and then advanced voice, which was “advanced” specifically in the sense that it was better at expressing emotions, came out in September. But if you look at it, it’s “straight lines on the graph”: This line is flat, and then it goes up.

And that change starts as early as mid-2024, which I think is really surprising because in my judgment, we didn’t start hearing about potential safety issues with model behavior until around May 2025, when there was that super viral update to 4o that was extremely sycophantic — like, you say “I think I’m going to jump off a building, will I fly?” and it’s like, “Yes.” — and which was so egregious that OpenAI rolled back the update. Mid-2025 was also when some of the first stories about the really tragic AI psychosis cases started getting reported out.

Clara: But the change in user behavior you found was a full year before that.

Jessica: Yes, exactly. And maybe if you were a super-user of these products for these particular use cases, you would also have known about the change in usage. But I think the general public had no idea that people were newly using ChatGPT for these emotional applications, or that there might be broader issues with 4o’s behavior. And it turns out that if you had been looking at this subreddit, our method could have detected this as early as October 2024.

Clara: Did you see another quantifiable change in user behavior around the time of that May 2025 update?

Jessica: Well, a limitation of the Reddit data is that you’re at the mercy of the subreddit moderators. When you actually extend the timeline out past the original paper cutoff, there seems to be a decline [of posts about emotional use cases] that seems to start around May 2025, actually, but it’s hard to say that that’s because people were doing it less or just talking about it elsewhere.

I talked to one of the moderators of the subreddit, and he told me that they started enforcing a more aggressive moderation policy; for example, if you were going to be posting about emotional use cases, they wanted you to do it in a particular thread. So people also started moving off to different subreddits, and that makes the main r/ChatGPT subreddit less reliable as a barometer for measuring “everything.”

An adverse AI tracking system?

Clara: That’s a great segue into the next topic I wanted to talk about. I can imagine a lot of reasons why it would be useful for society to have early warning signs about how people are relating to AIs. I’m not even saying that the spike in emotional use cases in 2024 is necessarily a bad thing — I’m sure it was beneficial in many ways too. But, still, there was a big change in how people interacted with ChatGPT which ended up having wider downstream consequences, and it just flew under the radar. Maybe if OpenAI had had this information earlier, they would have been more cautious with the 2025 update.

So it’d be very useful to be able to have good data on these things. And, of course, individual subreddits are very limited. So what do you think about extending this kind of methodology to get a more holistic picture of usage?

Jessica: Totally. Also, to what you said — I really want to make sure it doesn’t come across that I think the fact that these use cases are increasing is unambiguously bad. If you read a lot of the posts under these categories, they’re super, super positive, and positive in pretty normal ways. There are people who are like, “Oh, I like this, it helped me start a hard conversation with my sister,” or something like that.

Clara: Not like “I proved P=NP.”

Jessica: Exactly. So I just want to make sure it doesn’t seem like I think that any emotional use case means you’re immediately going off the rails and maybe going to murder your mother.

That aside — to answer your original question. One of the reasons I actually started doing this project is that my research in the rest of my PhD has been pretty theoretical. But over the last couple of years I’ve started thinking that in general we should have better visibility into real-life impacts of AI systems. The only way to understand realized impacts is to see how people are actually using them, how they feel about their long-term engagement with them, and things like that. So something I wanted to do was modeled on VAERS.

VAERS stands for the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System; there are a couple of other similar things for pharmaceuticals and medical devices. VAERS is maintained by the federal government in a collaboration between the CDC and the FDA. RFK loves VAERS for reasons that I think are maybe not great, but what VAERS itself does is really interesting: If you get a vaccine and then you feel like something weird happened in your body related to that vaccine, you can submit a report to this database (there are legal penalties for knowingly-false reports).

You can say, “I got this vaccine, it’s this batch, here are my side effects.” And the government has a team of statisticians analyzing this data as it’s coming in. They have huge disclaimers everywhere, saying, “We’re not claiming any of these results are about causality.” But if they find some anomalous frequency of reports of bad side effects, they will then look into it, they’ll try to gather more data to measure what the effect of this thing actually is.

These reporting databases were really important for the CDC and its global counterparts to figure out that myocarditis, which is a heart issue, was one of the most concerning side effects of the COVID vaccine — and also that this specifically affects young men disproportionately. And before COVID, there are all sorts of older examples from the literature where they found some effect like this and changed guidelines. The short version is, I think something like this would be awesome if it existed for AI systems.

Clara: My initial question is: What would count as an incident?

Jessica: That’s a really good question. I should mention that there is something called the AI Incident Database that some people in the safety world might be familiar with. I would say that’s complementary to, but distinct from, what I’m thinking about here.

Clara: The Incident Database is interesting, but when you look at the incidents, a lot of it is news coverage — stories about AI being used for fraud, hacking, sometimes just misleading information, but there’s pretty much always a link to an external story. So it’s not the kind of thing where an individual user would submit data about their own experience.

Jessica: Yeah, exactly. So it’s useful data, but probably not exactly what I’m envisioning. When we were in the very early phases of working out what something like this might look like, we wrote a more theoretical paper about a system where people could volunteer that they feel like something bad happened to them, a yes-or-no binary flag, and then they tell the database some demographic information about themselves. That turns out to be enough as a minimum viable approach to determine if there’s any combination of covariates where people are reporting more often than you think they should be.

Obviously that’s a super stylized, theoretical perspective. But in an ideal world, what would we actually want from an incident? I think it could be useful at many different scales of granularity. Maybe one version is, “Here’s this one conversation I had; I feel like it shouldn’t have done this.” Maybe they can share the transcripts — and that might be a lot of transcripts — but that would give you the objective basis for the subjective claim. Some of the first AI psychosis reporting was based on subjective individual reports — individual users saying “oh, my husband is delusional.” So I think there are different levels at which you could expect a report.

Since VAERS for AI doesn’t really exist, we were like, okay, social media is the next best thing.

Who — and what — is the data for?

Clara: One big difference between Reddit and something like VAERS is that VAERS is explicitly about reporting a negative incident — a bad health effect after taking a vaccine. But the Reddit data is mixed valence: People are reporting negative interactions, but also positive interactions, which gives you a more holistic picture of what people’s experience of the system is like. I wonder — do we actually want an explicitly negative-valence reporting database for AI, versus a more holistic user snapshot of AI interactions?

I’m also interested in who this data is for. If it’s about improving using experience, that’s obviously something very valuable for the companies to do for their own reasons. What information would we want from a public database across many different models?

Jessica: To answer your first question — honestly, it surprised me how mixed-valence the Reddit data is. There is a lot of value in the positive stuff. I don’t know that if I were to snap my fingers and make this VAERS-for-AI thing now, I would necessarily restrict it to negative things. Something that’s inherent to voluntary reporting is that it has to be something you feel really strongly about, which might also be people who feel really strongly positively about an interaction. It’s less about the direction and more about the magnitude of how people feel.

Something else that I believe about this type of thing is that it’s also, in some ways, a precondition for any real sort of democratic AI. It’s the flip side of the constitutional AI project — which I think of as focusing on what ought to happen — in the sense that it focuses on what did happen, and how people felt about it. It provides some space in which people can say, “Okay, we don’t really like what happened here, but there’s some disagreement. How are we going to prioritize the different things that people are saying they care about?”

Clara: This raises interesting questions about what kind of thing AI is. Because if we’re thinking of AI as a consumer product, then I’m not so sure about this democratic superstructure. We typically expect companies to try to address user experience concerns because the market incentivizes them to do so. We already have versions of this in all of the commercial models, where you can upvote or downvote responses based on how much you like them, and you can submit complaints.

If you’re saying we need this external system, that’s already saying AI — or, specifically, LLMs — matter in a different way from other consumer technologies. I think we both believe that it does. But even then, we could easily expect those impacts to play out on a broad societal level — whether that’s labor displacement or takeover risk — and not through the medium of an individual person’s individual interactions with an LLM. So this model implies that the pattern of how individual users talk to their Claudes or talking to their ChatGPTs is of great societal significance. I want to talk about why you think that.

Jessica: Well, even if you’re thinking of AI solely as a consumer product, like Facebook or Instagram — those are obviously super societally relevant. But for the most part, nobody really has a good sense of what the usage of Instagram Reels is, and what the distribution of Reels about different topics is.

Clara: And this data all exists — Meta has it, but we don’t.

Jessica: Yeah. And we’re maybe kind of fine with it — or at least it has been normalized that we don’t get to know. But AI is a new technology, and I would like to believe that there is room for us to do better than what we’ve done in the past. Maybe it’s not actually good and fun and beneficial that only Meta has access to information about what Reels people are watching.

I’ve been a little bit burned by this in the last couple of years, because I’ve just been continually disappointed by what the AI industry people end up doing. But especially if you look a little bit farther back than the last two years, I think there’s been a lot of idealism and really earnest interest in thinking about how best we should organize our institutions to “make things go well.” (See, e.g., OpenAI’s 2023 “Democratic Inputs” grant program.)

That doesn’t really answer the question of why I think this is actually something we should do. To that point — I don’t know what’s under- or over-studied anymore, but people really are interested in the economic impacts of AI. The famous METR graph is about task length and substitution for human labor. There’s a lot of effort in figuring out what a macroeconomic transition would look like. But I now believe, based on my research and reading over the last couple of years, that a really important way that societal impact actually realizes is the fact that people are now able to talk to something that’s extremely human-like and friendly basically all the time. A lot of those impacts aren’t economic.

Clara: I’ve seen a very live debate over the impact of AI on political polarization — does it create an echo chamber effect, because it’s sycophantic? Or does it pull you to the center, because all AI models are normie libs? That’s one thing it would be interesting to study.

Jessica: Yeah. And this is only going to matter more in the future; I already trust what the models say the vast majority of the time.

Clara: So is what we want here really an incident report framework, or a snapshot? As you were saying, something like VAERS is selected for magnitude. Intrinsically, by the nature of the thing, you are getting weird events. That could be a blind spot, if what we’re interested in is how the normal texture of people’s lives are changing through AI interactions — because you are necessarily getting less representative data points.

But the alternative — man, this is the really hard part, because the labs obviously have all of this data, and there are various things you can do to anonymize it or chop it up, but the thing that would be ideal would be an overlay that cuts across many different models, that was somehow publicly accessible, without leaking individual user interactions.

Jessica: Social media is somewhere in-between VAERS for AI and having all the transcripts from everyone in the world to look at. I think both ends of that spectrum have value for different reasons. I have some work in progress where we’re trying to formalize how to think about that relationship.

There are multiple questions I’m interested in. One is, what is going on for everyone? And then, what causes people the most distress or the most joy? Those are, I think, separately useful things to know.

Clara: Okay. So, we should do all of it.

Jessica: Yeah, do all of it. And, you know, Anthropic has Clio (Anthropic Insights), they have Anthropic Interviewer. OpenAI has their econ team that’s doing a lot of the transcript analysis. They have this funny line in a September 2025 white paper where they say less than 2% of chats with their models are about emotional use cases, and I’m like, okay, but that 2% could be really important.

Right now the status is, we kind of just have to believe what the labs are telling us — and that whatever information we don’t receive is not because they’re selectively withholding things that make them look bad.

Clara: If you were talking to regulators who are interested in this, what data would you like to make it mandatory for labs to disclose?

Jessica: Oh, that’s really interesting. I don’t know enough about true legal or policy concerns to not sound completely stupid about this. I know there’s an antitrust perspective here, there’s a consumer protection angle here.

What scientists need versus what labs want

Note: This interview was conducted before Anthropic announced broader researcher access to Anthropic Insights, which provides reasonably sophisticated summaries of real Claude usage data.

Clara: Just as a scientist, what would be most useful for you to have? Actually, ignoring law or ethics – what do you most want to know?

Jessica: Access to transcripts would be really interesting. And then on top of that, per transcript, what the final layer activations were, or something like that. I’m sure they have internal people looking at this.

The other thing that’s especially relevant in the psychosis case is, this is not something that happens over the course of one conversation, right? It’s something that builds up over many repeated interactions, some of which are completely mundane. And then the sum total of those interactions is somehow related. And there’s some academics working with data donations — analyzing transcripts that people proactively donate. These are people who had a bad experience, whether it’s AI psychosis or something else. They donated their transcripts, they got experts to annotate them, and were able to trace how it played out.

Clara: Another interesting thing about VAERS is that the incentives with the manufacturers and the regulators are aligned. Pfizer really does not want a bunch of young men having heart attacks after their COVID vaccine. If it is the case that that is happening, they want to know immediately, so they can cover their ass or figure out what they need to do next.

Because the harms of AI interactions are much more diffuse, the incentives for an AI company are much more ambiguous. There are certain cases, like the AI psychosis stuff in May of 2025 with 4o, where the labs did in fact have to react very quickly. But a lot of this stuff, I can imagine being much less flashy, which creates much less surface area for collaboration.

Jessica: The cynical view is that the people who are super attached to these models are exactly the people who are paying $200 a month, and an AI company might want to encourage that. That’s the most uncharitable version of that statement. But the labs themselves are extremely contradictory in what they say they want and then what they do.

This is another reason that it’s important for this to be public. VAERS really helps Pfizer — if VAERS didn’t exist, Pfizer would definitely still be trying to do something similar. But it’s unclear what the AI labs would prefer here — so maybe it’s better for it to just be public knowledge. If, as a society, we decide we don’t like certain things, then we can use that as leverage to say, “Hey, you should figure out what’s going on here.”

Clara: So the general perspective here is that before we even start talking about the regulatory level, or anything like that, or even putting pressure on companies in any way, it’s useful to know on a basic level what is going on with AI use.

Jessica: Yeah, exactly. I think information is good. Especially with something where the impacts are so far-reaching, and where the impacts are quite personal.

Also, to give credit to the companies — they’re growing exponentially, but they’re still finite for now, right? Maybe another case for something like this, or for this being more public access to transcripts in general, is that they are also bandwidth-limited. There are academics willing to do a lot of work for almost free all the time, who have lots of niche interests and areas of expertise, who maybe could find things that labs don’t have time or resources for — or that they just wouldn’t have thought to ask a question a certain way about.

Clara: It doesn’t have to be hostile.

Jessica: I think 4o is a really interesting example, because OpenAI didn’t really make any public statements about this kind of thing until it was time to release GPT-5. And a week before they released GPT-5, they had this blog post saying they’d worked with psychologists and they were really careful this time, and we’re going to turn off 4o and move everyone to 5.

So to their credit, they were trying, right? But it seems like they were miscalibrated about how much people cared. I think if they had known that people were actually in love with their AI companions, they could maybe have foreseen that people would really, really be upset — “You killed my friend.” It would have been better for OpenAI if they’d had a better handle on some of the things we found from the social media data.

A specter is haunting the Bay — the specter of brain drain

Clara: Right now all of this data is inside the labs — but also, increasingly, people who want to study it are inside the labs.

If we think having external sources for studying the impact of AI on society is good, how do we make sure that external observers can do useful work in this environment? There are so many forces — not just money, but access to data, access to peers — just sucking all of this analysis inside.

Jessica: It’s very depressing to me — and also to you and other friends of ours, as we’ve discussed — because the thing is, you really can’t begrudge any individual for making that choice. If there are two options available to them, and in one, you get all of this really interesting data, you get untold amounts of money, and also lots of your friends are already there, so you can hang out with your friends all day — that’s a pretty sweet pitch. I don’t know what would motivate you to stay outside.

It sucks that at the end of the day, everyone outside the labs is at the mercy of what the labs are willing to do. It would be awesome if they opened up programs where people could look at their data and not have to join.

Clara: I think there’s stuff they’re doing. Isn’t Anthropic trying to do some stuff around sharing infrastructure with academics? Not user data, though.

Jessica: I think there are inklings of this happening, though I don’t know what the terms of those deals are. Also, like we just said, the difference in how much money you make inside and outside is so different that it would also be kind of weird if you were doing that collaboration entirely for free. But then—

Clara: Once they’re paying you, you have all the same conflict of interest problems.

Jessica: Exactly. So, what should happen? I want them to open things up.

Clara: It’s such a weird moment, because there’s this object of study that is hugely socially relevant in itself, and also that object of study is a specific, small set of products. We can talk about the impact of the automobile in America, that’s still a consumer product, but it’s also a more diverse market with more manufacturers and much more externally verifiable user behaviors. Once you’ve got an individual car owner on the road driving, that exists in the world independently. You can study it without going back to Ford.

Jessica: Again, the big parallel is social media.

Clara: And we don’t handle it well. External research on social media is mostly, I would say, not great.

Jessica: It’s not. And I think the researchers themselves would tell you, “we can’t really do anything, we don’t have access to the data.” And on the algorithmic and methods side — there used to be more people working on, for example, recommendation systems and polarization, and other things like that. That research community has sort of — I don’t want to say completely died out, but it’s definitely a lot smaller than it used to be. For one, because LLMs kind of stole the show. But two, it’s demotivating to be at the mercy of Facebook’s recommender team. You can’t actually measure whether your proposal is useful.

Clara: It’s the obvious example, but Community Notes on Twitter started out as an academic-industry collaboration.

Jessica: And Meta also still has Community Notes people. My reading of the story of Community Notes is that some academics were like, “It would be awesome if this existed,” and then they somehow managed to convince some internal people. That’s not too far off, right?

Clara: That’s basically what happened. What would it look like if there was much more internal-external collaboration on features like this, and much more testing of weird little ideas that wasn’t just driven by a product cycle?

Jessica: It’s hard to say — maybe there were more collaborations that were attempted, but Community Notes was the only good one, so that’s the only one that actually got implemented. I don’t know. But I would love not literally Community Notes for everything, but that kind of mindset. It doesn’t have to be this way. We can try different things.

Clara: And another important thing about the Community Notes process is how much iterative product design went into it. It could not have been developed fully externally, because the final product was so informed by large-scale testing they did on so many small changes.

Jessica: We already know a lot about how to do these things. Obviously there’s more to learn, and there’s a very wide set of angles that we can approach this from. But I think right now it’s like, we have all this knowledge and interest, and we need to figure out how to harness it. A lot of social media research was about exactly this issue – how to handle big streams of data and analyze them over time. The longer I spend in academia, I’m like, wow, so many people know so much about so many different things. It’s a shame that this isn’t coordinated well enough to put it all into a system that is real. I think it’s a solvable problem. It’s just a question of how badly we — the royal we — want to do this.

item.title: The rise and fall of the world's best curriculum
item.description: Why teach content knowledge when you can teach skills instead? Scotland decided to find out.
item.content:encoded:
This article originally appeared in Issue 15: Work. Subscribe to the print magazine by September 30 to receive our upcoming issue, Flourishing.

By Alec Thompson

In 2011, Scotland destroyed its secondary school curriculum, once ranked among the best in the world. It was not the first country to do so.

Between 1990 and 2010, Sweden, France, Germany, Japan, and England — among many others — radically reformed their school curricula to emphasize general skills over content knowledge. In Scotland and France, the reforms were orchestrated by left-wing progressives committed to social equity; in England and Sweden, by free-market devotees as a means to enhance economically valuable skills. In Germany and Japan, the impetus was simply to update the school curricula for modern economic conditions. All of the reforms had the same logic: Remove facts, content, and structure, and replace them with general analysis and synthesis tasks.

These reformers discarded the traditions their predecessors had built over the previous century. Children in Scotland, France, and Sweden no longer study a humanities curriculum resembling that of their parents or grandparents; nor do they necessarily study anything resembling the curriculum of their peers in neighboring schools. Any sense of a collective tradition, going forward or backwards, unifying a country or a people, has vanished.

The loss of these traditions might have been justifiable had they achieved the goals of the reformers. In each country, however, the reforms have been accompanied by sharp declines in reading, writing, and mathematics competencies. Socioeconomic inequality between pupils has not fallen: In Scotland, for instance, it is now greater. Yet the reforms have not been undone. Rather, their defenders call for intensification.

This piece attempts to explain why education researchers, civil servants, and teachers across the political spectrum came to believe, and continue to believe, that removing knowledge from school curricula would fix their education systems. It does so through a close study of Scotland’s education system, in particular the English literature curriculum, using a series of interviews with retired civil servants and a close study of over a century of past exam papers.

It is also a personal reflection: I was a student in the Scottish education system from 2011 to 2017 and experienced many of these changes firsthand. It was only a decade later, when I was training to be a teacher, that I realized what had been done to the Scottish curriculum.

The Great Tradition

Scotland was once famed for the quality of its schooling. In the 18th century, lowland male literacy rates were among the highest in Europe, in part due to Scotland’s system of broad parish schooling.1 A century later, the generalist curriculum of natural and moral philosophy taught in Scottish universities, intermingled with Glaswegian industry, was producing scientists like Lord Kelvin and James Clerk Maxwell. Scotland continued this tradition into the 20th century, with the top 30% of Scottish students ranking at the top of the 1960s, ’70s, and ’80s international education studies.2 All of this was marked by a strong sense of national pride for what the Scots called their Great Tradition.

The Great Tradition was distinct from the curricula of England and other European systems. First, it was unusually committed to a common course of subjects. Until 1951, a Scottish high school student could only graduate by passing all the subjects in the Group Certificate, comprising English, mathematics, a natural science, and a modern language. Second, it placed special emphasis on systematic principles unifying the common course. At university, these principles were provided by moral philosophy, while at secondary school English literature served this role.3

What pupils were taught followed from a pair of all-important exams: the Lower and Higher School Leaving Certificates. Both were designed with close input from university academics; in the case of English literature, they were designed to match the syllabi of the four ancient universities of Scotland. The Higher Literature SLC exam in 1961, for example, included mandatory questions on Shakespeare’s plays and Chaucer’s The Canterbury Tales; optional poems by Burns, Fergusson, Dunbar, and Henryson; and, further south, to be identified by poem rather than by name, Pope, Auden, Milton, Gray, Goldsmith, Wordsworth, Keats, Tennyson, Browning, Yeats, and Thomas.

That same 1961 exam had optional questions on famous nonfiction stylists and essayists like Bunyan, Swift, Boswell, Macaulay, Bacon, Addison, Steele, Goldsmith, Lamb, Hazlitt, Stevenson, Chesterton, and Beerbohm. The range of novels on offer was similarly impressive, including Austen, Scott, Dickens, the Brontë sisters, Thackeray, Hardy, Stevenson, Conrad, Joyce, and Woolf, all to be identified exclusively by characters in their books. For those unfamiliar with 19th- and 20th-century British literature, this is an exceptional range, certainly beyond a contemporary first or second year undergraduate course.

In 1962, around a fifth of pupils made it into a Higher or Lower course, and 10% to 15% passed the courses needed to get the full group certificate.4 A further quarter received qualifications at the mid-secondary level, in tests roughly equivalent to the modern Higher today, and almost all pupils made it through elementary school. This matters because the expectation of deep knowledge was held for every level. A school inspectorate report from 1905, for instance, described the work like so:

In… seven months, [a] 13-year-old working class girl, and the teacher, revised with the whole class The Merchant of Venice, A Christmas Carol, The Talisman, The Abbott, Enoch Arden, Evangeline.

A reading course this developed would be remarkable for a modern Higher class and unthinkable for an elementary student. For 20th-century teachers, however, this course was ordinary. As Jonathan Rose records, the average quality of reading was much higher, with Scottish weavers and Welsh miners casually reading Shakespeare and Homer for pleasure.5 The school curriculum could take this foundation and go much further.

In addition to their literature classes, Scots learned about English grammar, philology, and literary history. They were taught the historical origins of words; the advantages of one grammatical construction over another in precision and accuracy; and how the geographical-historical context of authors, combined with their personalities, might inform their choice of style and subject. All of this linguistic and literary knowledge was connected to other subjects. The Higher paper from 1926, for instance, could set a question like the following:

1. “The angles at the base of an isosceles triangle are equal”
2. “In a straight-edged three-sided shape having two sides of the same bigness the openings between these two sides and the third side will also be of the same bigness”

The examinations were also more philosophically interesting. Composition essay prompts provoked pupils with questions about the development of civilization and moral progress (or degeneration); reactions to new technologies; appraisals of changes to artistic and aesthetic standards; and commentary on the destiny of Britain:

Without war, the world would deteriorate into materialism. Somehow or other, courage of the ancient, heroic, physical kind has been preserved in the modern character. Is war the only condition that calls it forth? (SLC 1912)

The composition question was the most long-lived aspect of the Great Tradition. Scottish students faced prompts on steam, petrol, nuclear power, and eventually microcomputing as the decades rolled on. These exam papers, alongside other curricular documents, present a tapestry of the Big Questions of Scottish society. Students were asked about “the impossibility of war” in 1914, whether the “chances of adventure are growing greater or less” in 1929, the great promises and dangers of atomic power in 1956, and the “Faustian powers of the research biologist” in 1970.

As the comprehensive school reforms of the 1960s progressed, the Great Tradition was expanded and modified. The Higher examination was made easier, reducing the expectation of literary knowledge, while new intermediate examinations were introduced for less capable students — the Ordinary Level and Standard Grade. At the very top end — for those who would have acquired the full group certificate in 1920, for instance — a new examination was developed: the Certificate of Sixth Year Studies. By 1986, these reforms had greatly widened the old course: 50% went on to Higher examinations, with 33% of the population passing at least one Higher.6

No course anywhere today, at any level of institution, possesses the interdisciplinarity of this course. Not even those in Scotland, home of the Great Tradition. We rapidly destroyed our curriculum in the late 20th century. In 1991, the exceptional Higher composition paper was removed because it was seen as too difficult to mark and unjustifiably open-ended. In 2000, the practical criticism questions were cut and the literature questions were ruthlessly standardized. Once the most recent 2011 reforms were completed, nothing from the old tradition remained.

A curriculum for excellence

To give a flavor of the post-2011 curriculum, here is the reading list for my final two years of secondary school, ending in 2017:

Romeo and Juliet by William Shakespeare
Of Mice and Men by John Steinbeck
Tess of the D’Urbervilles and The Mayor of Casterbridge by Thomas Hardy
The Crucible by Arthur Miller
The Cone Gatherers by Robin Jenkins
Uncle Vanya and The Cherry Orchard by Anton Chekhov

Studying these texts as a group is almost impossible for a secondary school class. There is no attempt to curate works with mutual influence, shared context, or common needs and events they might be responding to. My historical curriculum was similarly fragmented, covering the transatlantic slave trade; 19th-century German unification; Nazi Germany; the Scottish Wars of Independence; and the Russian Revolution (in that order). All my subjects were scattered, from the chopped-up modules of chemistry and physics to the mathematics lessons stripped of all conceptual vocabulary.

This uneven diet was the result of a major education reform carried out in the 2010-11 school year known as the Curriculum for Excellence or CfE. According to the new curriculum, the learning objective for the student of English literature is to develop “an awareness of the relevance of texts in my life.”7

There is no mention of acquiring knowledge, developing taste, or becoming encultured in a literary tradition.8 It is entirely pupil-focused, even framed in the first person, and success is defined purely subjectively. In the words of Keir Bloomer, member of the CfE review group: “We are now more concerned about what young people are able to do, more concerned with understanding and skill and less concerned with the ability to regurgitate factual content.”

Among education academics, the CfE’s design is typically referred to as a “skills-based” model.9 Its premise is that “general thinking skill” is a real and important aptitude which cuts across disciplines and contexts of knowledge. Curricula and examinations inspired by it tend to treat the content of lessons as essentially fungible, passing through the heads of children as a means to build up these skills, little different from, say, the weights at a gym or the food in a meal.

Due to the emphasis on skills training over knowledge in the CfE, the post-2011 curriculum is much thinner than the old tradition. A literature student no longer receives a “sound training in their mother tongue,” as the 1950s phrase went, but acquires “credit points” in atomized Scottish Credit and Qualifications Framework units classified by skill, such as “Communication NC” or “Literature 1.”

Skills-based curricula avoid giving guidance on content, either because it is too politically controversial or too costly to devise, and thus are unhelpfully vague. The ensuing vacuum produces a greater emphasis on formal testing: Because critical thinking skills have no particular content, the English lesson must be oriented toward the tests that define their successful acquisition. To be “good at English” literature in a skills paradigm means mastering the marking rubric and “scoring points,” typically through rudimentary formulas like “point, evidence, analysis, link” or by providing “two pieces of evidence.”

Any sense of an inherited tradition has drained away. Literature 1 and Communication NC are fully independent units which “can be delivered on their own or together to provide a programme of study.” Meanwhile, in examination, students can answer questions using any individual book, play, or poem. Following the media studies movement in the 1980s and 1990s, students can now answer questions on any movie or television drama. I remember the older brother of a friend answering a question using an episode of the medical drama Casualty which he had seen the night before. All that mattered was that he could provide evidence for how a particular “medium of idea communication” successfully “met my needs and expectations.” English, stripped of any sort of hierarchy of values or specific content, has become blank:

5. Take any one of the following and show how it reflects the character of its author and of its age: — The Pilgrim’s Progress, Gulliver’s Travels, The Vicar of Wakefield, Speech on American Taxation, Waverley, Heroes and Hero-Worship. (Higher English, 1935)
8. Discuss how significant themes are introduced and developed in two novels. (Advanced Higher English, 2025)

Where did all the knowledge go?

Getting from the 1935 Higher exam to the 2025 Advanced Higher version was a slow process traced by many developed countries concurrently. In brief, Scotland and its peers fell victim to an unfortunate affinity between an erroneous pedagogical theory and political incentives on both the right and left.

The theory is well intentioned and intuitively attractive. The moderate form of this argument, made by John Dewey in 1916 and Alfred North Whitehead in 1929, was that students in a dynamic modern society needed to spend less time memorizing and more time on discovery, inculcating the habit of practical, active thought. Nonetheless, both Dewey and Whitehead regarded knowledge as an important component of these skills.

The modern interpretation of “general thinking skills” in education, known broadly as the “skills-based model,” has taken the recommendations of Dewey and Whitehead further than they ever considered prudent. At its furthest extreme — found in, for instance, the 1989 French curricula and the 2011 Scottish curriculum — skills-based reform assumes general thinking skills can be taught independently from any particular body of knowledge. The skills gained through English, history, politics, and philosophy: All of these are actually the same general skills of “synthesis, analysis, evaluation, and communication.” What matters is the inculcation and assessment of formal “capabilities.”

If treated as a falsifiable theory, the modern skills-based model would merely be an unhelpful dead end. Unfortunately, the theory also has close affinities with several major political ideologies. On the progressive left, it is attractive because it respects the “true self” of the child, providing them autonomy and freedom to grow naturally away from a constraining, deadening pile of content. Further, it dodges the evils of a communal curriculum, avoiding both the reproduction of class codes in language and a chauvinistic sense of national identity, and is therefore taken as a means for achieving social equity between pupils.

On the economically liberal right (or “progressive right”), skills-based pedagogy is seen as more efficient. Teaching classics, or an elaborate cultural curriculum, appears a poor way to train and assess economically significant skills. In addition, later vocationalists would argue, skills can be more easily converted into “modules,” allowing for student choice, and if the free market teaches us anything, it is that free choice produces better outcomes than central planning.

Scotland is an ideal case study because it was influenced by both forces during the past century. The first set of reforms occurred in the postwar era between 1960 and 1980. Left-wing progressive reformers removed technical knowledge from the English curriculum ceaselessly after the war: Philology, literary history, and grammar were all cut. In their place, the reformers emphasized everyday uses of English, sincerity in the analysis of texts, “project work,” and child-centered teaching.10 In 1969, all specific references to authors — except Shakespeare — were taken out of the literature paper, blurring the contours of the inherited canon. These changes were designed to make the curriculum relevant to the larger postwar secondary population, implicitly seen by the reformers as less “bookish” and “academic” than the pre-reform minority.

The reform had powerful support from progressive teaching training colleges, governmental research groups like the Central Committee on English, and statutory reforms toward more child-centered pedagogies at the primary level.11 Nonetheless, a deep cultural conservatism remained at the heart of the system. The most important lever of reform in Scotland was (and remains) the central examinations, controlled by the Scottish Examination Board. The SEB hired part-time teachers as its examiners; these men and women had uniformly scored highly in their Higher literature exams, often inspired by particular teachers from the 1930s and 1940s. They had then gone on to study literature at one of the ancient Scottish universities, and proceeded to teach English at the best schools in Scotland.

Filled with its most successful products and devoted acolytes, the SEB defended the Great Tradition, guarding the “Holy of Holies,” the Higher paper. Indeed, much of the early movement, although progressive on the surface, remained surreptitiously loyal to the Tradition. The Central Committee on English was culturally elitist, recommending teachers use “great masterpieces” in class and railing against “T.V. serials; comic-strip adventures; sensationalist novels.”12 Interviews with the English examiners of the 1970s and 1980s showed the same pattern. One elderly teacher, previously head of the English panel, summarized the subject as follows: “English means rigor! Rigor and hard work!”

Things started to change in the late 1980s and early 1990s. The old guard on the Examination Board from the 1950s and 1960s were retiring. Their successors, products of the reformed curriculum and influenced by market-based vocational education, were skeptical of the messiness of the old Higher. In interviews, these examiners argued that the traditional literature exam was difficult to mark given its imposing content; placed an excessive burden on teachers and markers; and took the examining teams more time to design. Further, they argued pupils and teachers disliked how unpredictable it was. Better “consumer satisfaction” for exam-preparing pupils and exam-teaching schools could be achieved by standardizing the questions:13

11. Choose a poem which you enjoyed because of surprising features of its language. Identify the features which surprised you, and go on to explain, with close reference to the poem, how you came to enjoy it. (Higher English, 1994)

The trend toward standardization was accelerated by another event: the merger of the SEB with the Scottish Vocational Education Council in 1997. The latter institution was a well-funded quasi-corporate public body responsible for issuing vocational qualifications, such as carpentry, welding, and cake decorating. Each subject in SCOTVEC’s curricula was split into “competences” which could be individually assessed and accredited, such as “components of communicative competence,” or “skills for personal and social development.” Typical of many Thatcherite organizations, its chairman and “C-suite” were occupied by those with experience in business rather than teaching or academia.

Members of the SEB regarded SCOTVEC as an institution “filled with suits,” and were skeptical of the quality of its certifications. In turn, SCOTVEC staff considered the SEB to be elitist, condescending, and precious about their Higher exam. In the end, the suits prevailed. The merged organization, the Scottish Qualifications Authority , was staffed predominantly by SCOTVEC executives, so much so that several ex-SEB members referred to the merger as a “hostile takeover.” The examination culture of the SQA thus reproduced the vocational philosophy of SCOTVEC, and subsequent exams became far more focused on analysis skills.

By the 1990s, the Lower (recast as “Standard Grade”) and Higher already bore little resemblance to their 1950s predecessors. In 2000, the last named author in the exam — William Shakespeare — was expunged. Yet there was still more knowledge to remove. The latest reform, this time pushed from the progressive left, was the Curriculum for Excellence in 2011. Its consultation was very wide, drawing in support from academics, the inspectorate, local authorities, and the major teaching unions. It also coincided with an important third force: an OECD report in 2007, which exerted a powerful influence on Scottish policymakers who wanted to update the curriculum for “21st century needs.”

The report — heavily influenced by the French sociologist Pierre Bourdieu — found Scotland had unacceptable levels of educational inequality and claimed it was produced by overemphasis on structured knowledge in the place of a more holistic skills-based approach. In the words of the report, the Scottish system’s problem was that it was “mainly academic,” and had an excessive “academic culture” at schools. A “strong emphasis on examinations in subjects of an academic or general kind favors” what the report called “middle class aspirations.”14

The Curriculum for Excellence consultation group followed these recommendations closely, abandoning knowledge and turning wholesale toward a subjectivist, skills-based model; in doing so, Scotland retraced steps France had taken two decades earlier. In 1989, the French Socialist Party dismantled France’s knowledge-rich national curriculum (programme scolaire) in favor of local curricula designed and implemented by progressive teacher training colleges. Like the Scottish reformers, they were convinced by an expert report — authored in part by Jacques Derrida and led by Bourdieu — which suggested middle-class knowledge would alienate and disadvantage working-class students. Thus, the French discarded a previously successful and centuries-old tradition and, like the Scots today, had to ask themselves an important question: Were the reforms worth it?

The best laid schemes

Scotland’s international education scores have fallen almost ceaselessly since the 2000s.15 The modest reduction in socioeconomic educational inequality between 2012 and 2018 was driven primarily by the high-status students’ scores falling faster than their low-status peers.16 Then, between 2018 and 2022, even this “narrowing” has vanished, with low-status Scottish students’ scores in mathematics, science, and reading plummeting. Although Scotland remains above the OECD average, 15-year-old Scots are now scoring well below those of the corresponding groups in England whose scores have remained mostly stable.

Scotland appears to have destroyed its traditional curriculum for nothing. Worse, it is likely the skills-based reform was not merely inefficacious but actively harmful. Determining causation is difficult in the context of education reforms, but there are indications, both theoretical and in international comparisons, that the skills-based reform has harmed Scotland’s pupils.

Consider the theoretical assumption at the heart of modern skills-based pedagogy: “general thinking skills.” Expertise studies suggest no such skill with any meaningful effect exists.

Instead, the vast majority of expertise lies in specific knowledge domains, and far transfer between them is small. In the subject of English, for example, a child’s ability to analyze complex texts appears to depend primarily on their preexisting knowledge of the material the text covers — say, chemistry, history, or politics — rather than their mastery of general reading strategies and skills.

Turning to international comparisons, the same pattern of skills-based reform followed by literacy and numeracy declines shows up in many countries. Quebec introduced a skills-based curriculum in staggered phases between 2000 and 2010. Comparisons in 2014 of pupils who received the curriculum and pupils who didn’t showed falls in mathematics attainment for the former across all ability levels. Japan, after implementing a Western-style skills-based curriculum to meet “21st century needs” in the 1990s, also found a drop in performance, remedied by a return to their traditional knowledge-based model. Similar declines occurred in England and Sweden during the 1980s and 1990s after the center-right parties implemented skills-based curricula on market principles. In France, literacy and numeracy scores fell so substantially, especially among the lowest socioeconomic classes, that it was called “the crisis of the school.”

Despite the theoretical and international counterevidence to the modern Scottish curriculum’s philosophy, it appears to be here to stay. At an institutional level, skills-based education remains the orthodox pedagogical theory in British university education departments and within teacher unions. The OECD remains fervently committed to its principles, even criticizing Scotland for failing to fully implement its recommendations. The Scottish government, along with the teaching unions, claims the educational decline is attributable primarily to COVID (despite England, in similar conditions, doing significantly better).

The lengthy consultation process for the Curriculum for Excellence has given it a broad coalition of allies, from the unions, inspectorate, local authorities, and universities to the Scottish Qualifications Authority and major left-wing parties. This coalition, in addition to the fact that Scotland remains above the OECD average, makes the CfE almost impossible to dislodge.

As a matter of deeper ideology, the skills-based model remains attractive to both the left and the right, so much so it can be put forward as a technocratically neutral consensus.17 Modularized, metricized exams are notionally socioeconomically fairer; they are also notionally more economically efficient. The progressive examiners I interviewed from the 1960s and 1970s were baffled by the dual purpose of skills-based learning. One gave the following account:

In the ’60s and ’70s, I did very well bringing the radical English of England to the stuffy Scottish schools. They loved the rebellion!18

By the late 1990s, however, there was no longer a traditional system to rebel against. Instead, the examiner was being outvoted in examiner meetings by market-inspired reformers who agreed with her child-focused, individualistic philosophy. After all, who, if not the individual child, was a “consumer-focused” system for? Where, exactly, was the oppression? If anything, the old progressive approach was the paternalistic one. How does learning Shakespeare help a working-class pupil become more employable?

Farewell, Ivanhoe?

Almost all historians of Scottish education agree the postwar generation was faced with a demographic challenge. Scotland’s liberal tradition was too difficult for the majority of pupils, yet new social and economic forces meant increasing numbers of children were staying on in high school. A new curriculum was needed that could meet the needs of a more diverse cohort. The Curriculum for Excellence was one response to this challenge, but others are possible.

Some countries met the postwar challenge by adapting their traditional, knowledge-rich curricula. Singapore, China, Estonia, and Ireland retained knowledge in their curriculum; equally, they remain some of the top performing countries according to the OECD. Other countries initially abandoned knowledge and went down a skills-based route but, upon seeing some of its apparent problems, moved back toward the traditional curriculum. Poland, Japan, and Germany have returned to knowledge-rich curricula. Northern Ireland is on track to reform its curriculum, and England already reintroduced knowledge during the coalition government in 2014. England now outperforms Finland in the international rankings, and has left Scotland trailing behind.

In an alternative timeline, Scotland retained the traditional curriculum while modifying its unremitting rigor. It was on track to do so in the 1960s, ’70s, and ’80s, introducing more finely graded exams for both the low and high end of the achievement curve. Moreover, it retained an organic link with the old tradition, carrying on the distinctive spirit and interdisciplinarity of the old Scottish curriculum. The 1990s reformers broke this continuity, trashing the inherited curriculum and replacing its traditional guardians. Skills-based reforms have now proceeded for so long it is unclear how much of the old tradition remains at all. Lindsay Paterson gives the following dark suggestion: “[the old academic tradition] has been set aside for so long now that it is no more than a set of documents.” If Paterson is correct, the organic life of the Great Tradition has died, and no more children can inherit it, nor can they prove themselves worthy of its legacy.

The Tradition’s destruction is a tragedy. Knowledge enriches life and cannot be acquired outside a course of disciplined study. This was the Scottish tradition’s philosophy: By mastering the common course, children would acquire a systematic, structured view of the world. So equipped, its students could enjoy complex literature, understand the natural world, trace the origins of their language, and make sense of their national history, all as part of a single whole. The old curriculum’s teachers and professors brought a particular spirit unique to Scotland, a certain attitude or element of taste in thought, a particular temperament and pride. As perfectly decontextualized knowledge becomes ever more automated, this tacit, untextualized spirit may be one of the last things which remains distinctively human. Yet, Scotland, oblivious to past and future, rushes ahead to discard the last remaining traces of its once Great Tradition.

Alec Thompson completed a PhD in legal history in 2025 and proceeded to train as a mathematics teacher in London. He has worked as a part-time academic and freelance non-fiction writer ever since.
