item.title: The unacknowledgeable work of pastors’ wives
item.description: Help Wanted: Someone to be everyone’s friend.
item.content:encoded:
By Elizabeth Van Nostrand

This article originally appeared in Issue 15: Work. Subscribe to the print magazine by September 30 to receive our upcoming issue, Flourishing.

Before I was interested in pastors’ wives,1 I was interested in pastors. Specifically, I got nerd-sniped by church planting, the evangelical domestic missionary system that furthers its members most sacred quest (introducing more people to Jesus) while honoring their need for independence. The resulting system resembles nothing so much as Silicon Valley startup culture, where young, charismatic, ambitious men fundraise from the community (and especially former founders) in order to start churches that have a 90% chance of failure but a 1% chance of astronomical success.2

Like startup founders, church planters have a robust podcast ecosystem. I spent dozens, if not hundreds, of hours listening to them talk with each other. One frequent topic was how hard planting was on their wives and children. Planters work the hours of a surgeon with the pay scale of, aspirationally, a teacher. Wives are often called upon to contribute a great deal of their own time to the church. But what most interested me was the amount of work that was required of pastors’ wives that could not be acknowledged as such.

Pastors’ wives, especially at new and small churches, wear a lot of hats. On any given day they might stuff envelopes, run A/V equipment at a service, or compile the monthly books. People being what they are, this work often doesn’t receive as much acknowledgment as it deserves, but it is usually acknowledgeable as work in the abstract, in the sense that everyone is fine saying that the tasks took effort and were done to achieve a result, not for joy of the process (although they’ll still expect you to iron 25 angel costumes with no notice and instant turnaround).

But some of the expectations of a pastor’s wife come with a meta-expectation that the task be done out of sincere love and be rejuvenating rather than tiring. Greeting people after services is not supposed to be work the way stuffing envelopes is; it’s supposed to spring out of the joy of meeting new souls and hopefully bringing them to Jesus. She doesn’t have to attend four church events a week, she gets to (and it reflects badly on her relationship with God if she feels otherwise). She’s not a social worker helping a client, she’s a friend honored that you trust her with your secrets. Asking for these tasks to be acknowledged as effortful-but-worth-it, and not enjoyable for their own sake, ruins their emotional impact. And because a pastor’s wife’s (unpaid) job is to create that emotional impact, this would make her a failure at that job. The social work of a pastor’s wife is not just unacknowledged by the congregation, it’s unacknowledgeable.

Pastors’ wives aren’t the only people facing this problem; there’s a lot of feminist theory on invisible and emotional labor. And every parent has an appreciative role to play on Mother’s Day or Father’s Day regardless of how much damage their two-year-old did in the process of making them breakfast in bed.

The unacknowledgeable work demanded of pastors’ wives is the large-print, easy-to-read version of a problem that constantly annoys me.3 To understand this work, I went down a second rabbit hole of pastor-wife podcasts,4 written material, and four interviews with women from nondenominational churches.5

Who is she?

There is no hard data on this, but based on my original podcast survey, church-planting pastors were sometimes cradle Christians but often came to Jesus in high school or even college. In contrast, pastors’ wives6 (at least those who go on podcasts) seem to be almost universally cradle Christians, and a disproportionate number are the daughters of pastors.

From my listening, a common story emerges: A pastor’s wife most likely met her husband in high school, possibly at Vacation Bible School, and married in or shortly after college. He probably knew he wanted to be a pastor, and she probably knew she wanted to be a pastor’s wife, often since before she knew she wanted to marry him in particular. If a woman feels called to ministry within evangelical Christianity, wife is the primary path offered to her.7 There is a separate demographic of pastors who don’t feel the call until middle age, whose wives are considerably less enthusiastic, but they don’t go on podcasts about it.

In a small 2017 survey, 55% of surveyed pastors’ wives8 worked outside the home and church, and the number would be higher if you excluded the mothers of very young children. Almost all PWs want children, but most in this survey stop at two or three. According to Olivia, the wife of a pastor of a large southern nondenominational church, pastors’ family sizes are often limited by financial constraints. Finances are one reason pastors’ wives so often work outside the church, but many view their work, often in education and medicine, as a calling and ministry,9 not just supplemental income.

Undeniable friendship

Olivia enters every supermarket on alert. Like a gregarious Terminator, she continuously scans her peripheral vision for anyone hinting they might know her. At the suggestion of recognition or eye contact, she locks eyes and smiles warmly.

She does this because she knows of other pastors’ wives who missed eye contact from a parishioner, maybe even frowned because of something heavy on her mind, and later found out the parishioner went home hurt and angry that the pastor’s wife was ignoring her. (At least she wasn’t accused, as others have been, of being demon-possessed by someone who didn’t like her 1,000-yard stare at the gym.) Not only has she hurt that woman’s feelings, but if she misses enough of these opportunities, she’s guaranteed that someone will decide she’s stuck up and uncaring and everyone in church needs to hear about it. Even people who know a PW lost a parent four days earlier will chastise them for crying during services — but they’d better be unremittingly sad after a pregnancy loss, when experiencing any joy at all would be inappropriate.10

The demands of friendship go beyond brunch and painting each other’s nails. Sometimes what people really need is therapy, but they don’t have a therapist; they have you.11 This is hard enough for pastors, who might have a semester of counseling training from seminary. Wives rarely have even that. This leaves them potentially lacking both in the straightforward skills of helping people and the subtler skills of protecting themselves while doing so.

Unreciprocal fellowship

Okay, so pastors’ wives are required to be everyone’s friend and confidant. That sounds like hell to me, a grade A introvert, but many people thrive on having as many friends as possible, and a role that lets them speedrun emotional intimacy is a blessing, not a burden.12

However, true friendship requires reciprocity, and this is mostly denied to pastors’ wives.

She is expected to have the church be her primary social outlet, but every church member is a little bit her husband’s boss. Complaining about marital problems more severe than her husband’s former difficulty putting away his socks (but he’s much better now) undermines him and endangers his position in the church. Pastors have been fired because their wives complained to the wrong person(’s wife). Many wives on many podcasts acknowledge the difficulty of raising kids with a partner who works such long and erratic hours, far away from family,13 but it was only after talking to Mike Riggs, the grandson of a long-serving pastor, that I learned of his grandmother’s hatred of the way certain female congregants overvalued her husband’s attention and the structural difficulty her husband had turning them away.

Not everyone needs reciprocity in their friendships; some people thrive being the Giving Tree, in which case the hurt comes when the recipient stops letting you see the fruit of your work. Families leave churches for lots of reasons — doctrinal disputes, an out-of-state job, needing a bigger program for their children than your tiny church can provide. Or maybe your husband’s role is cut for budgetary reasons, and the congregation is too embarrassed to face you. If any of these happen, the default outcome is that you never hear from the women you helped again.14

Three decades ago, Margaret spent five years as the wife of a pastor at a church with 50 to 80 members, three of whom invested in helping her while she was there — and one of whom continued to socialize with her after she initiated a divorce.

All of this leaves the pastor’s wife constantly pouring her heart out into people who don’t refill her. If she is lucky, she will have childhood friends she can rely on and be a part of a strong peer-support group for PWs.15 There, she can complain about unresolved marital problems, critical parishioners, and her own struggles with faith without worrying she’ll hear about it next Sunday.

Unavoidable pressure

No mom lives free of mommy-war judgment, but many moms can reassure themselves that it’s not personal and the judges can’t hurt them. Not so for pastors’ wives. The entire congregation is noticing your toddler’s post-service zoomies, and some of them are absolutely sure you and possibly the elder board need to hear about it. You might hope this would stop as the kids grow up and move away, but no, parishioners view your adult daughter’s family planning as fair game. You not only need to hear their opinions but must do so gracefully, because responding with anger or even annoyance reflects poorly on you and your husband.

The social demands on pastors’ wives don’t end with being everyone’s one-way friend. If a PW is lucky enough to have true close friends, especially if they’re in her church, she needs to keep it on the down-low because other women in the congregation will get angry they weren’t included. Carrie Pankratz, the wife of a nondenominational pastor in Utah, refrains from posting innocuous pictures of girls’ brunch on social media to prevent jealousy.

In the PW podcast world, discussions of financial difficulties are common. According to Olivia, the goal of most churches is to pay their lead pastor like a local teacher, but many can’t afford even that. If you are somehow able to afford an extravagant lifestyle, you’d better refrain, because something as innocuous as a family of five buying a used minivan can be viewed as showing off. What podcasts don’t talk about, but pastor’s grandson Mike Riggs and ex-PW Margaret did, is that looking too poor is also cause for judgment. It can make you look unskilled at budgeting or perhaps disfavored by God.16 Margaret’s husband wouldn’t let her apply for the food stamps they qualified for because it might make the church feel bad about underpaying him. Hope your family is healthy, because illness is also evidence of God’s disfavor.

Sometimes the pressure is not from judgment, but just reality. Families with young children won’t attend your church if you don’t have a children’s ministry. Running a children’s ministry takes a competent, trustworthy person. You might not enjoy running Sunday school, but do you hate it so much that you’re willing to let your church fail over it?

This is how Allison — whose husband is the lead pastor at an independent church of roughly 200 attendees — wound up becoming the finance chair at her husband’s church, despite her own disinterest and a glaring conflict of interest. The alternative was to risk the church dying due to the inability to fill the role. Allison is eagerly awaiting her husband’s retirement. But until that day, the church is important to her husband, and she would rather volunteer than let the church fail.

Immeasurable rewards

Multiple friends I discussed the question with guessed that being a pastor’s wife was desirable because it conveyed a lot of status. Mike confirms that this was a source of satisfaction for his grandmother (whose husband retired in 1995), but Margaret confirms that even three decades ago, the role came with more demands than respect.

When I look at the role as it stands today, all I can think is “there has got to be an easier way.” Being a culturally white pastor’s wife endows a woman with a lot of trust and attention, but these mostly bring more work and expectations. To my mind, status is supposed to protect you from other people’s demands, not create more.

When the women in question speak in public, the most common reason given for becoming a pastor’s wife is that “it advances God’s plan” or “God called me to it.” I think irreligious people often underestimate what a strong reason this can be — similarly, I keep using the word “unacknowledged” when, from their perspective, the only being who truly matters is tracking every moment. And since evangelicalism, particularly the Southern Baptist Convention, mostly closed nonmatrimonial paths to ministry for women in the ’90s and early aughts, pastor’s wife is the role to apply for if you want to invest in a domestic church.

Some women truly love the work. Olivia described being a pastor’s wife as having “a front-row seat to God’s work.” She didn’t have to take a maladjusted young woman into her home or bail her out of jail; she got to, and her reward is seeing that woman grow and thrive and pay it forward as a foster parent to teen moms. Margaret quit the job of pastor’s wife (via divorce) after six years but spent the next 30 loving being a social worker. There were many things she disliked about being a pastor’s wife, including being taken for granted, but the multitude of opportunities to support others was not the problem.

There is, of course, the question of how sincere these answers are. My cop-out answer is that there certainly are women for whom these are their true reasons — Margaret has no congregation to impress and three decades of evidence that she genuinely enjoys social work — but it’s impossible to know what percentage, because other answers would be unacceptable and imperil their husband’s position. If the unacknowledgeability didn’t protect itself, it wouldn’t stay unacknowledgeable.

I focused on smaller podcasts, which featured women talking with their friends. Larger, longer-running podcasts tend to feature mostly women with books, retreats, and merch to sell.

By Asterisk Magazine

It’s a dark and confusing world out there, and sometimes the hardest part is trying to figure out what’s going on. Our future is being decided in group chats you’ve never heard of. Members of technical staff are filling the timeline with cryptic warnings, and everyone you know has an opinion on third-party AI evaluations.

We can’t claim we’ve never been part of any shadowy cabals,1 but we still like to dig up dirt. That’s why Asterisk’s Winter 2027 issue is Secrets. Don’t go telling everyone, but we’re particularly interested in the following topics:

  • Group chats, underground networks, and how the culture of secrecy affects everything else

  • Arms race dynamics, and whatever is going on at the labs

  • Niche or obscure histories, oddly influential but underrated arcane knowledge

  • National security, cybersecurity, and physical security

  • Taboos and open secrets

  • Genetics and medical privacy

  • Covert operations, bribery, and secret money

  • Persuasion, deception, manipulation, and cover-ups

  • The unconscious and the collective unconscious

Our magazine pieces tend to be long (3000 to 5000 words on average), evergreen, and deeply researched. We welcome pitches and drafts from everyone, not just academics or professional writers.

Email us at submissions@asteriskmag.com by October 31. Write a few paragraphs explaining the idea, how you would complete the essay (which sources would you reference? is it reported?), a target word count, and a little about yourself, including any relevant expertise.

We will reject all pitches that include AI-generated text. Due to the volume of submissions we receive, if you do not hear from us within two weeks, please assume that we have passed.

In confidence,

Clara, Angela, and Nadia

item.title: The right (and wrong) worries to have about water
item.description: And what we can do to improve the situation.
item.content:encoded:
By Lawrence Costa

In grade school we were taught that water is a renewable resource that covers most of the planet and, quite literally, falls from the sky. I remember water cycle posters from second grade: a storm cloud that dropped rain in the mountains, which collected into rivers, which flowed into lakes or oceans, whereupon the water evaporated to form a new storm cloud. The point was that water moves through this cycle but is never used up. Despite that immutable bit of Earth science, modern society has long been preoccupied with the fear that our water resources are on borrowed time, as though we might accidentally turn the entire planet into a desert.

This fear is pervasive in mass media. The movie Chinatown was released in 1974 and the villain who secures a monopoly over life-giving water has since become an archetype. In Rango from 2011, the rich water thief is an evil folksy tortoise. James Bond gets in on the trope in Quantum of Solace. The 2015 film The Big Short is ostensibly about the 2008 financial crisis but ends with an ominous description of investors shifting their focus to water.

If these examples speak to a moderate anxiety, more apocalyptic options are available. There are now five Mad Max movies set in Australia, with water becoming more precious in each iteration. In Tank Girl from 1995, you can watch Malcolm McDowell rule a desert world — Australia again — and kill his enemies by desiccating them with a spiky suction cup (apropos of nothing, that movie is partially animated because they somehow forgot to film about 10 scenes). In the New York Times bestseller The Water Knife, water rights — which can apparently be carried around like bearer bonds — are worth killing over and somehow still enforceable in a dystopia.

In public policy discussions, our fears can manifest in odd ways. We worry about almond farming (a thirsty high-value crop) but not alfalfa (a very thirsty low-value crop). We worry about evaporative water loss from data centers in Virginia (a region with a near inexhaustible supply of fresh water) but we also put water-guzzling golf courses in Phoenix (a desert).

How did we come to be so incoherent? We worry about a crisis that doesn’t exist while doing very little to reform water management institutions. Less panic and more moderate bureaucratic change (riveting solution, I know) could make us richer while improving the environment.


Importing each other’s water problems

For most of human history, freshwater concerns revolved around agriculture. Things were fine as long as there was enough water to grow crops. Some cultures, like the Khmer Empire, came up with ingenious solutions for water management but were still undone by changing weather patterns. Often, however, civilizations arose in areas where the supply of water relative to possible uses was effectively unlimited.

This was the case when the eastern U.S. was first settled by Europeans. One didn’t need to worry about water at all since the amount available was so vast relative to any possible use for it. In fact, as the historian Anthony Carlson describes in Perilous Waters, we spent many decades preoccupied with draining freshwater wetlands to create more farms. The term “reclamation” initially referred to reclaiming swampland, rather than reclaiming water for arid regions.

The military explorers Stephen Long and Zebulon Pike popularized a notion that the Great Plains were a “great American desert,” incapable of supporting agriculture.

The situation changed with the turn of the last century, when we became capable of fouling water at scale. Our first foolproof plan to deal with water pollution was to ignore it. As described by the historian Mike Wallace in Greater Gotham, New York City’s industries operated on the assumption that tides simply carried away any pollutants. The city tested this with dye at one point, realized it wasn’t true at all, then… kept dumping sludge in the rivers. Today, some of the city’s waterways are EPA Superfund sites and the billions of oysters that once lined its bay are long dead. Despite localized disasters, society maintained the belief that we couldn’t possibly damage water resources at a large scale. One could simply go to Long Island to see clean water.

It was in the drier West that we had to worry about getting enough water for the first time. The military explorers Stephen Long and Zebulon Pike popularized a notion that the Great Plains were a “great American desert,” incapable of supporting agriculture. Pike especially was relieved due to his concerns that American democracy might not be sustainable across too vast a geographic expanse, noted historian of the American West Patricia Limerick in an interview.

Humans turned out to be ingenious engineers and simply built our way around nature’s constraints. Water is seasonal in the West, so in the 1800s we began assembly of a vast infrastructure to store and distribute it, eventually enabling large-scale agriculture. We were so enthralled with our success that we seemed to forget any constraints existed.

In the early 20th century, western water reclamation projects — this time, with “reclamation” coming to mean capturing and retaining water, rather than draining it to make swampland arable — kicked into high gear. Eastern congressmen were initially “not willing to tax the farmers” of their own states to take western lands “and convert them into sugar-producing lands.” But opposition was short-lived and congress created the Bureau of Reclamation in 1902. By the 1930s, the government was addressing agricultural surpluses on one hand (by paying farmers to take land out of production) while, with the other, building reclamation projects that would put more land into cultivation.

Meanwhile, the East and West seemed eager to import each other’s problems. It was puzzling enough that Eastern cities consistently placed sewage lines next to their freshwater intake sites, according to Limerick — but it was even more strange that, learning nothing from the failures back east, Western cities did the same, ending up with their own pollution issues.

Nonetheless, there was an unshakable belief in engineering our way out of anything.

Mistakes, mistakes, mistakes

So it happened that optimism veered into recklessness. Nationwide, we polluted with abandon, exemplified by the time Cleveland set the Cuyahoga River on fire in 1969 — the “mistake on the lake” — and managed to get a Lake Erie reference in the Lorax by doing so. (Point of fact, we set that river on fire at least 13 times, but the 1969 one received national attention.)

Out West, it was as though any sort of water conservation counted as defeatism. The tragedy is that this era’s engineering feats were remarkable! We built an industrial economy and did manage to enable farming in a region that should’ve been too dry for it. But then we deluded ourselves into thinking we’d never have to care about where our water comes from.

In Science Be Dammed, Eric Kuhn and John Fleck describe how, starting with the Colorado River Compact in 1922, we’ve consistently allocated more water than the river has. Crucially, this was never an honest mistake: Before the compact was signed, U.S. Geological Survey hydrologist E.C. LaRue famously warned that water level projections were being rosily based on an unusually wet period. He was ignored.

Even more gob-smacking examples of self-deception are available. The Dust Bowl by Ken Burns explains how farmers fatuously assumed bumper rains would last forever during the anomalously wet 1920s. They undertook a “Great Plow-up,” tilling vast tracts of prairie grasses — which had adapted to uncertain rainfall over eons — and replacing them with drought-intolerant crops. The resulting ecological catastrophe was the second time the region’s homesteaders got burned: In the 1800s, they’d told themselves that “rain follows the plow” (i.e., planting a region will make it rain there) until an 1890s drought proved them wrong.

The problem of water quality first captured national attention insofar as it affected drinking water. In The Search for the Ultimate Sink, historian Joel Tarr explains that water quality was seen as a public health problem and “solved” by treating only our incoming drinking water. Of course, treating drinking water made us much healthier (I, for one, am happy to have never had cholera), but it did nothing to keep industrial waste from our waterways.

Out West, it was as though any sort of water conservation counted as defeatism.

If anything, it made that problem worse because it meant less political pressure on polluters. Things shifted by the middle of the 20th century, as society came to view water pollution more in environmental than epidemiological terms, thanks to new and more visible chemical pollutants, like synthetic organic chemicals that could add thick layers of foam to rivers.

We became gradually more conscious of the problem of water scarcity as we ran out of low-hanging fruit for irrigation projects. Sensibly enough, the best western reclamation sites — dams, reservoirs, irrigation canals — were built out first, so each additional one was more and more marginal. By the 1970s, additional projects just didn’t make any financial sense; by the 1980s (the canonical book on the topic, Cadillac Desert, was published in 1986) we started to see the downsides of our century-long water management spree. These drawbacks included mineral accumulation on irrigated land, pushing animal species to the brink (it’s very difficult for salmon to spawn in a dammed river), and overdrawing the Colorado so persistently that it would no longer reach the sea.

Also, we just got richer. This explanation for why we started to care about water management (and any environmental issues really) can be attributed to more than a few academics, notably among them historian Samuel Hays and economists Gene Grossman and Alan Krueger. Perhaps that’s because it’s obvious in retrospect: A wealthier society has more attention and resources to devote to the environment. It’s easier to care about whether salmon can spawn when one isn’t worried about contracting typhoid from the municipal water supply.

We began to fix our mistakes. On pollution, the Clean Water Act in 1972 marked the point where we got serious about the problem. The act federalized standards, imposed limits on “point sources” of pollution (e.g., a “point source” might be the pipe dumping sludge from a particular factory), and it provided vast sums of money to fund municipal sewage treatment.

On scarcity, there was no, shall I say, watershed moment. Rather, there were various marginal changes that made an impact over time. Urban areas made real progress on demand management, so much so that total usage fell despite large population gains in the southwest1. Federal plumbing standards helped in this regard. (Anyone who has come across the odd dive bar with a pre-standards-era toilet can attest that they use something like an Olympic swimming pool worth of water to flush). Additionally, some water was reallocated from agricultural to urban uses, and farmers began to use water more efficiently (though there is still much work to be done on both of those fronts).

As a result, water quality today is much better than in the 1970s. Water scarcity is still an open issue, but the West has managed to avoid essentially all of the dire predictions from the 1980s: Instead of running dry, cities greatly reduced per capita water use; aquifer depletion didn’t make farming impossible so much as force us to substitute crops; the speed of sedimentation (which fills in reservoirs making them ineffective over long timescales) was vastly overstated; and salinization of farmland proved to be something of a manageable headwind rather than a catastrophe.

The trouble is that our perceptions are stuck in the era of burning rivers. Pollution is still a concern everywhere, but these days mostly from agricultural runoff, which looms large now simply because we’ve been so successful at addressing industrial waste. Outside of periodic droughts, water scarcity is mostly a concern in arid regions. Even in arid regions, and even with climate change, there is a vast amount of water available. Conservation is good for the environment and, in the long run, would make farming more sustainable, but cities just are not going to run out of water for human consumption.

What’s left to worry about today?

So, what exactly are the water management problems we face today? I sat down with several resource economists and a water policy specialist to find out.

Brian Gray, an expert on water law at the Public Policy Institute of California, told me that the federal Clean Water Act and state-level water quality laws have significantly reduced municipal and industrial water pollution, at least from his vantage point as a California specialist. Nationally, we’ve seen a marked improvement as quantified by researchers David Keiser and Joseph Shapiro.

That said, an improvement does not imply full success. As a New Yorker, I’ll note that the Gowanus Canal remediation has been in progress for nearly two decades and the plan for mitigating the city’s combined sewer is scheduled for geologic timescales. My sarcasm aside, Gray stressed that the federal law explicitly exempts agricultural sources of pollution (i.e., runoff) from regulation because these were thought impractical to measure (being diffuse rather than “point” sources of contaminants).

Agricultural pollution mostly entails phosphorus and nitrogen; these aren’t industrial toxins but the ecological impact is quite large. The EPA rates over 40% of streams in poor condition for these nutrients, which harms wildlife (the chemicals cause algae blooms, which can, among other things, leave water hypoxic). The effect on human health is more difficult to quantify: It’s unclear exactly how bad high phosphate exposure is and it can be tricky to measure how many people are exposed. That noted, exposure rates seem to be small and concentrated among households with private wells.

These constitute a gap in our remediation efforts but there’s cause for hope on that front: Gray said that many farms, especially in California, use canals and pipes for drainage, which makes tracking pollution more feasible. California, for one, is beginning to regulate these discharges under state law.

The resource economists I spoke with — Eric Edwards at UC Davis, Nick Hagerty at Montana State University, and Jonathan Yoder at Washington State University — all focused on Western water rights, simply because water scarcity, while occasionally an issue in the East, is ubiquitous and more severe in the West.

A common refrain from them was that it is often enormously difficult to actually trade water rights, meaning that even though the arid West still has a lot of water, an overly complex system makes us inefficient at allocating it. Simplifying the process would make it easier for cities to grow, allow farmers to profit from the sale of their water rights, and would allow us to leave more water for the environment.

Briefly, a water right is the right to do something with a water source. The right may specify use (e.g., consumption of water, diversion of a stream, etc.), point of use (that is, exactly where the water may be drawn), quantity of water, return requirements (how much water must be returned to the source after use), and so on.

In the U.S., water rights fall into two main categories: The first is riparian, under which water rights are tied to land abutting a water source; with this regime people are allowed “reasonable use” and rights are usufructuary, meaning land owners have a right to the water but do not legally own it. This type of right is the default in the East.

The second category, prior appropriation, is common in the West. Under that doctrine, rights are not tied to the land. For instance, one may own a plot of land but not have the right to place a well on said land — to do so, you’d need to purchase the relevant water rights. Prior appropriation rights are based on seniority, which means, if I ignore a lot of nuance, one owns a senior right if he or she happens to have an ancestor who first came along and put a water source to a “beneficial use”. Riparian rights tend to work best where there’s a lot of water to go around, which explains why the West uses a different doctrine.

Riparian rights are straightforward: One acquires the right with a parcel of land. So the market for them is just the land marker. Thus, when we talk about water markets, we’re usually referring to prior appropriation rights. In a prior appropriation water rights market, one may theoretically purchase rights to water, but the process is rarely straightforward.

Edwards explained that if a large city wanted to increase its water supply, the matter isn’t so simple as just using the municipal budget to purchase water. For one, many farmers have water rights but cannot sell them because rights are often collectively managed by water districts that coordinate among farmers. If the city finds willing sellers, the two parties cannot simply agree to the transfer. Other farmers could protest that changing water diversion patterns would impact them. Such issues often end up in court. The process is so Byzantine that water brokers exist to work through the bureaucracy, and, of course, they have to be paid.

The end result is a huge gap between what a buyer pays for rights and what a seller might receive. Yoder said the economic literature is “full of transaction cost estimates” estimated to be roughly 1/3 the value of a sale.

In some places, it’s not just transaction costs and market frictions gumming up the works. The Colorado River Basin is perhaps the biggest water management problem we have right now. Yoder noted the initial over-allocation means that we’ve just fought over the water rights since. It’s difficult to even talk about transferring water rights if there’s uncertainty over which states’ initial claims will win out. How can something be transferred if we can’t even agree who controls it?

None of the economists advocated a completely deregulated system. After all, a large share of western water disbursements are managed by the federal government. Plus, when we talk about trading water rights, we’re often considering public entities acquiring them from one another. Does a public utility in Phoenix need a given amount of water or should it go to a public utility in San Diego? The point is that a functioning market for water could allow the cities to trade effectively (with each other and with farmers), ensuring neither suffers in a drought.

What of more science-fiction sounding solutions? Perhaps we’ll succeed in making electricity so cheap that large scale desalination is practical? Well, no. Hagerty allowed that it’s a “potentially exciting option, particularly valuable for reducing urban water uncertainty, but depends a whole lot on how cheap electricity could get.”

But, water is heavy and slippery and, thus, expensive to transport. Even if desalination were free, piping it from the coast for agriculture would be hugely expensive relative to moderate changes in our water management institutions. Hagerty added that, right now, having to use desalination in California represents a “huge policy failure” because it’s just so expensive relative to the water we already have. It seems working amicably together is still our best option for managing the most salient of natural resources.

Overall then, our water management problems can be attributed to misaligned incentives and rickety market mechanisms. Boring bureaucratic details. So why, instead of reasonable technocratic changes, were people being hectored to stop drinking almond milk a few years ago? Why are the papers filled with articles about data center water use now? Why so much paranoia? And, above all, why do people seem to worry about a lack of water instead of a misallocation of the vast amounts of water we already have?

Yoder suggested a status quo bias, explaining that soda-pop bottling plants have faced local resistance too. People worry about new water withdrawals. The specter of a single “data center” industry also gives a nationalized face to what were once just various local fights over commercial water use. At my prodding, Yoder agreed that the public “often lacks a sense of scale.” Hagerty said, “one of the biggest problems is that a lot of journalists are not quantitatively literate.”

In an effort to prove myself the exception, here’s some arithmetic: The thirstiest data center in the world uses about 1 billion gallons of water per year by evaporating it for cooling. (It uses the same type of HVAC system as large apartment or office buildings) That’s enough to grow about one square mile of alfalfa, which is used for cattle feed. That amount of feed would translate to getting about 500 head of cattle to slaughter weight, not counting feed for the breeding herd. There were over 27 million head of beef cows in the U.S. at the start of this year and the U.S. grows over 22,000 square miles of alfalfa each year.

Now consider our most-stressed large water system. The Colorado River Basin flows at, on average since 2000, 12.4 million acre-feet of water each year, or over 4 trillion gallons. The difference between a billion and a trillion is difficult for humans to comprehend, but a billion seconds makes just over 31 years, a trillion makes over 31,000. We consume 13.1 million acre-feet from the Colorado.

The gap we need to close is actually less than 0.7 million acre-feet because of inflows along the river. This isn’t an insurmountable problem; it’s 114,000 cows; we have 27 million of them, not counting milk cows, the breeding herd, and calves.

I asked Edwards, Hagerty, and Yoder about their outlooks for our future. Since we’ve already reclaimed just about all the water we feasibly can, Edwards explained that the available water is a zero-sum proposition but the value we get from it certainly isn’t. “I think there are 1,000 different things people would do to become more efficient, from switching crops or deficit irrigation at low cost all the way up to high cost xeriscaping and rain barrel installation,” he said.

Yoder mentioned policy options that can work well in some circumstances, such as water banks, which allow rights holders to forgo a water withdrawal and “bank” the right to do so in the future. He also sees promise in emerging technologies to reduce regulatory and transaction costs, which would make re-allocating water less cumbersome.

Hagerty focused on the status quo at first, explaining that, even in developing countries with institutions far worse than our own, authorities tend to act in time to ensure adequate water supplies. The counterexamples are well-publicized simply because they are so anomalous. He followed up to explain that we have the option of continuing as we have, but that doing might squander so much potential:

“I think we will continue to muddle through most water scarcity challenges despite our brittle institutions for water management, but I think a lot of these discussions are missing another big issue — it’s not just about how much urban areas will have to cut their water use, it’s also about what our urban areas could look like if more water were available for them. If we had more water, how much housing could be built in some of the most productive, most desirable, and lowest-emission cities in the country? How many people are missing the chance to have a better job, more opportunities, a better life? How many new cities would be built in the Southwest if there were more water for people? We don’t know exactly, but it might be a really big deal — it’s plausible it outweighs all the other problems we tend to think about with water management.”

For my part, I think our unrelenting negativity on this issue is almost the mirror image of our grandparents’ confidence. In both cases, many people have refused to engage with reality or admit that trade-offs must be made. One writer I interviewed for this piece was incredulous when I suggested we may need to set priorities between competing concerns, abruptly ending the meeting and asking not to be quoted here.

However, insisting that we focus on everything at once has a lot in common with refusing to worry about anything: Either way, we excuse ourselves from necessary action. The fact of the matter remains that theatrics — like banning data centers in water-rich New York — will not add one drop of water to the Colorado River. What’s more, there’s no arch villain trying to hold our cities’ drinking water hostage. The truth is more banal: Voters, and farmers, and policy makers are being a bit emotional and a bit short-sighted. We could make things easier for ourselves and the environment if we’d address water management like adults.

Lawrence Costa is an economist who writes about trains and operas on Substack because he lacks interpersonal skills. His research has focused on housing, labor markets, and education. He once went to Scranton (inadvertently).

1

There is a huge disparity between the value farmers place on water (low) and what cities do (relatively high). Cities could really use some additional water, but it’s a pretty reasonable amount; agriculture will remain the largest user by a wide margin.

item.title: How Zambia approved an HIV drug in 12 days
item.description: Sometimes, the access gap is not a scientific or economic problem.
item.content:encoded:
This article originally appeared in Issue 15: Work. Subscribe to the print magazine by September 30 to receive our upcoming issue, Flourishing.

By Enlli McAleese

Nearly three decades ago, Dr. Peter Mugyenyi, a leading authority on the treatment of HIV/AIDS in Africa, posed a question that has lost none of its sting today: “Where are the drugs? The drugs are where the disease is not. And where is the disease? The disease is where the drugs are not.”1

No matter how effective, a medicine cannot reach patients until it is authorized by their country’s medicines regulator. Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) often lack the staff, infrastructure, and expertise to independently evaluate new drugs effectively. As a result, there is typically a four- to seven-year delay, on average, between a medicine first being submitted for approval in a wealthy country and its final approval in sub-Saharan Africa.2

Take Zambia as an example.3 The Zambia Medicines Regulatory Authority has roughly 150 staff members. (For comparison, Australia’s regulatory agency, which serves only a slightly larger population, has around 1,000 staff.) Within the World Health Organization’s maturity framework, ZAMRA has yet to achieve level 3 (out of 4), indicating a stable, well-functioning approach to regulating medicines.4 Over 90% of the products ZAMRA reviews are generics.

So how did Zambia approve the HIV drug lenacapavir in 12 days?

The wonder drug

To understand why the race to approve lenacapavir matters, it helps to understand what came before it.5

Pre-exposure prophylaxis — PrEP — was first approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 2012 to prevent HIV infection. The standard regimen, a daily oral tablet called Truvada, works well. The problem is that it only works when people actually take it every day, and adherence at that frequency is hard to sustain, particularly in the communities PrEP is supposed to reach. One review estimated that fewer than 30% of people who started daily oral PrEP remained protected six months later, mainly due to discontinuation or inconsistent use.6 Stigma compounds the problem, since a daily pill is visible and implies something about a person’s risk profile to anyone who sees it.

Lenacapavir, developed by Gilead Sciences, is administered as a subcutaneous injection twice a year. Results from two phase 3 trials — PURPOSE 1 and PURPOSE 2, conducted across sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, Southeast Asia, and the U.S. — showed that more than 99.9% of participants remained HIV-negative during the one-year follow-up period. A twice-yearly injection neatly sidesteps both the adherence problem and the stigma problem in one go. By June 2025, when the FDA approved the drug for HIV prevention,7 Science magazine had already awarded lenacapavir its 2024 Breakthrough of the Year.

The question was how quickly it could reach the people who needed it most. Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for 65% of all people living with HIV globally, and 86% of children with AIDS. It also had the highest rates of discontinuation of oral PrEP. Whatever the merits of the drug, it would only matter if it could get through the regulatory machinery of individual countries fast enough to make a difference.

That was not guaranteed. When it comes to regulatory capacity, Zambia is not an outlier. Over 90% of African countries have limited or no capacity to independently evaluate new drugs.8 A submission to a regulator can sit in a queue for years. Gilead needed a different approach.

Trust me, I’m a reliable regulator

A full drug assessment involves many different kinds of work, including evaluating clinical trial data, reviewing manufacturing quality, assessing pharmacovigilance systems, and considering the benefit-risk balance for a specific population in a specific disease context. Some of that work is universal. Some of it is local.

The approach Gilead used — regulatory reliance — decomposes the task. The idea is that instead of requiring every national regulator to conduct a full independent review of a drug from scratch, regulators with fewer resources draw on evaluations already performed by trusted authorities elsewhere, then cover the remaining ground, such as the locally specific questions about their own populations, disease contexts, and health care systems.

A drug that has been assessed by the FDA, then the European Medicines Agency, then Health Canada, then Australia’s Therapeutic Goods Administration, and then 20 African regulators, has had the universal portions reviewed many times over by people doing essentially the same job. Reliance collapses that redundancy while preserving the locally specific judgments that only national regulators can make.

This might sound like rubber-stamping. However, even when a regulator draws on another agency’s assessment, it makes the final decision of whether to approve a product within its own jurisdiction, and takes complete responsibility for that decision.

When reliance works, it works well. It can cut review times by half.9 The limiting factor, however, is trust. How do you trust the work of others when you know it’s going to be your head on the chopping block if something goes wrong?

Trust is earned through demonstrated track records and formal vetting. The WHO maintains a List of Authorities — essentially a Michelin Guide for regulatory agencies that identifies regulators operating at an advanced level of performance. The FDA, the EMA, Australia’s TGA, Health Canada, among others are on it. These are institutions whose assessments you can rely on without having to independently validate the quality of their processes.

While the FDA and EMA are world-class regulators, their mandate stops at their borders. When they approve a drug, they approve it for their populations. Their benefit-risk assessments do not account for the disease burden and health care contexts of people outside the United States or the European Union. That’s why there exist specific pathways designed to build off their expertise and incorporate the needs of low- and middle-income countries. These mechanisms not only enable reliance on existing assessments, but generate assessments shaped around the populations that matter most. The EMA’s EU-Medicines for All (EU-M4all) procedure is one such approach. The WHO Prequalification Programme is another option. Between them, they formed the backbone of lenacapavir’s route to Zambia.

The relay

Gilead’s regulatory strategy for lenacapavir was, in essence, a carefully designed relay. Each step leveraged the work of the previous one.

Step one: the FDA. A submission to the U.S. regulator is the starting point for most drugs. In December 2024, the FDA placed lenacapavir under priority review, accelerating the standard 10-month assessment timeline to six. However, the reliance chain that would eventually reach Zambia began not with the FDA in Washington, D.C., but in Amsterdam with the EMA.10

Step two: the EMA. After submitting lenacapavir to the FDA, Gilead then went to the European Medicines Agency in February 2025, both for the right to market it in the EU and for an assessment under the EU-M4all procedure, previously known as Article 58.

EU-M4all exists specifically to provide rigorous scientific evaluation for medicines intended for markets outside the EU. The same committee that reviews medicines for European patients reviews the drug with the populations of target countries in mind, including local disease burden and health care system constraints. It is the same standard of assessment, applied with a different frame of reference.

A medicine’s benefit-risk profile is not context-free. A drug’s particular side-effect profile might be a better trade-off against a backdrop of higher disease mortality, or present different risks in a population with different comorbidities. For example, sub-Saharan Africa has extremely high rates of TB-HIV coinfection. This is an issue far less salient to a European reviewer evaluating a drug for European patients, but central to any benefit-risk assessment for the region where lenacapavir is most needed.

The EU-M4all process also brings non-EU regulators into the room before any downstream decision is required of them. For lenacapavir, experts from the WHO, Uganda, Zambia, Kenya, Nigeria, Zimbabwe, South Africa, Thailand, and Vietnam all participated in the assessment. They signed confidentiality agreements that entitled them to see Gilead’s unredacted trial data, the same data the EMA committee members themselves were reviewing.

A positive EU-M4all opinion is a signal to every downstream regulator in the chain. It tells them that a rigorous, internationally credible body has looked at this data with their populations explicitly in mind, and found it favorable. It is also an asset. The EMA committee publishes a full assessment report of EU-M4all’s opinion (lenacapavir’s was a juicy 206 pages), which becomes a shared resource that any regulator can draw on, rather than proprietary knowledge locked inside the walls of any single institution.

The EMA recognized lenacapavir’s urgency and reviewed it in 120 days rather than the standard 210. In July 2025, it issued a positive opinion.

Step three: WHO prequalification. Next, Gilead submitted to the WHO Prequalification Programme in August 2025.

WHO prequalification is a gateway to procurement. Most international purchasing agencies, like UNICEF and the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria, typically require a product to be WHO-prequalified before they will buy it. Getting on the WHO list is therefore not just a regulatory milestone, but often a commercial prerequisite for reaching patients at scale in low- and middle-income countries. Without prequalification, the drug may be nationally approved but still practically unreachable because the organizations with the purchasing power to distribute it at scale won’t buy it.

There are two routes to WHO prequalification. The first is the full prequalification pathway, in which the WHO conducts an independent scientific review of the complete dossier from scratch. This is the path for products without any prior approval from a recognized agency. Products approved via this route are eligible for the full Collaborative Registration Procedure, through which the WHO shares its assessment and inspection reports with participating national regulators and allows them to ask questions of the WHO during their own review.

The second is the abridged prequalification pathway. This is a streamlined WHO assessment for products already approved by a recognized agency, resulting in full prequalification status and the same Collaborative Registration Procedure eligibility. Until recently, this pathway was only available to medicines approved for use within the recognized agency’s region. This changed in March 2025, when new WHO guidance expanded the abridged pathway to include products only approved for use outside the recognized agency’s region (i.e., export-only), meaning those that had received a positive opinion via EU-M4all could now be included.11 Lenacapavir was the first product to use the expanded abridged prequalification pathway.

The abridged review does not reevaluate the clinical data. Its focus is confirming that the product submitted for WHO prequalification is identical in all material respects to the product assessed by the recognized agency. Is it the same formulation? The same specifications? The same packaging? To help answer these questions, the manufacturer submits the reference regulator’s assessment report (the European public assessment report in lenacapavir’s case) alongside product samples, quality documentation, batch records, and a letter from the agency authorizing the WHO to share its unredacted assessment and inspection reports with national regulators via the Collaborative Registration Procedure.

The fact that the WHO participated directly in the EU-M4all process helped considerably. By the time Gilead knocked on the WHO’s door with the prequalification dossier, the WHO’s assessors were not encountering lenacapavir for the first time.

Under the new procedure, the WHO can still request additional data specific to the safe use of the product in relevant regions beyond what the EU-M4all assessment covered. In the case of lenacapavir, the WHO asked Gilead for stability data demonstrating the product maintains its quality throughout its stated shelf life under Zones III, IVa, and IVb conditions: the high-heat, high-humidity storage conditions typical of much of sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia, which fall outside the climatic zones the EMA routinely requires data for.12

This all resulted in the WHO prequalifying lenacapavir on October 6, 2025. It only took it 36 days — roughly one-fifth of the FDA’s and a quarter of the EMA’s priority review.

The 12 days

At this point, it probably will not come as a surprise that Zambia’s regulatory agency did not review over 100,000 pages of technical data from scratch in 12 days.

The reliance architecture described above made it possible to sidestep that constraint without abandoning regulatory rigor. Zambia’s own experts had already participated in the EU-M4all process. They likely had already formed views on lenacapavir’s benefit-risk profile for the Zambian population. The EU-M4all process had, in effect, done a substantial portion of ZAMRA’s analytical work for them, months in advance.

When the WHO prequalification package arrived, it included not just the WHO’s own abridged assessment report but the unredacted EMA assessment and inspection reports. ZAMRA received everything it needed to make an informed decision without having to generate any of it itself.

So what exactly did ZAMRA do during those 12 days?

It verified. Gilead would have provided a declaration of “sameness” (that the product submitted for national approval was the same as what the WHO had prequalified) and a cover letter justifying any difference, which ZAMRA reviewed against the reference dossier. This is a repeat of the verification process that happened earlier in the chain. Each link requires its own check because the product could, in theory, differ between submissions.

ZAMRA’s own submission requirements also mandate that applicants submit physical product samples alongside a certificate of analysis, so a sample of lenacapavir would have arrived on ZAMRA’s desk.13 Furthermore, Gilead’s application needed to fulfill local requirements, which would include at a minimum local labeling review and any country-specific administrative or postmarket surveillance obligations. These tasks were answerable by a small team with access to the right documents in less than two weeks, precisely because the foundational work had already been done elsewhere.

On November 4, 2025, after 12 working days, ZAMRA approved lenacapavir for HIV prevention. ZAMRA’s approval time for new drugs via verification is usually over a year, but in this case it took one-third of the time the WHO itself took to prequalify it.

Regulatory reliance is working when each step in the chain takes less time than the previous one. In the case of lenacapavir, the gap between first submission and approval in Zambia was under 11 months.

The accumulation of trust

There is a managerial instinct, when faced with a decision that will be yours to own, to redo the underlying work yourself. The instinct is understandable, particularly when you are a regulator in a poor country, acutely aware of the consequences of substandard drugs. But the instinct, followed rigidly, is also what produces the access gap. Every redundant full review is a tax on patients who are waiting.

In regulatory reliance, the question moves from “Did we independently evaluate this drug thoroughly?” to “Do we trust the institution whose evaluation we are leveraging, and have we verified that what we are approving is the same thing it approved?”

The first question is unanswerable for national regulators that lack the resources to conduct their own thorough evaluation. The second is tractable when good reliance practices are followed, and the reliance machinery that supported Zambia’s approval of lenacapavir has been decades in the making.

The WHO has been the biggest driver of reliance mechanisms to support access to medicines in developing countries. The first such tool was implemented in 1969, when the WHO launched its Certification Scheme for pharmaceutical products, which allowed exporting countries to voluntarily issue certificates attesting to a product’s quality and manufacturing standards.14 This gave countries with limited regulatory capacity assurance about the quality standards of the medicines entering their markets.15 In 1987, the WHO created the Prequalification Programme, initially to help UNICEF with its vaccine procurement, before expanding to medicines in 2001. The EU-M4all procedure followed in 2004.

While the results of these programs have been meaningful, they are also uneven, and quantitative data on the adoption of regulatory reliance in sub-Saharan Africa and LMICs more broadly is extremely limited, partly because regulatory agencies in LMICs often lack the capacity to maintain data transparency around their approval processes.

The WHO has prequalified around 1,500 health products, and its Collaborative Registration Procedures, established in 2015, had facilitated 59 approvals across 23 countries by mid-2021, with 69 countries participating as of early 2026.16 However, the products eligible for prequalification are limited, likely due to limited capacity: The department overseeing prequalification had the same number of staff (approximately 115) in 2022 as it did in 2019, despite a substantially heavier workload.

EU-M4all has been slower to take hold. By 2020, only 10 positive opinions were issued. A 2015 EMA review of the procedure found that manufacturers doubted the pathway actually accelerated downstream approvals, maintenance fees were burdensome, and many national regulators either weren’t aware of it or treated it as a second-tier assessment. Coordination between the EMA and the WHO was also deemed suboptimal.17

Adoption has also faced structural obstacles on the part of the relying agencies. For example, certain countries still lack the domestic legal basis to formally practice reliance in the first place: You cannot build a review process around another agency’s work if your own legislation does not permit it. The African Union’s Model Law on Medical Products Regulation is one ongoing effort to give member states a legal template for doing so.

A subtler constraint is that effective reliance requires a sufficient degree of regulatory competence in the relying agency — verification is not an unskilled task. It is also worth noting that after approval, agencies must independently conduct postmarket surveillance, monitor local adverse events, and oversee national labeling and product information requirements. This points to a broader criticism: Reliance alone will not help agencies develop the capacity and local expertise needed in the long term, leaving them dependent on external assessments and ill-equipped to respond to domestic regulatory challenges. This is why the current WHO guidance on good reliance practices makes clear that reliance and sustained investment in local capacity must go hand in hand.

As this history attests, lenacapavir’s success was far from guaranteed. Lenacapavir benefited from an unusual convergence of factors. It had exceptional clinical trial results that made regulatory hesitation difficult to justify. It had a manufacturer with the resources and experience to navigate reliance pathways effectively. It had a preexisting access infrastructure built up over decades of HIV/AIDS advocacy. Not every drug will enjoy these benefits. The four- to seven-year average will not immediately become 11 months across the board.

But it is worth being clear about what the lenacapavir case demonstrates. It shows that the access gap is not primarily a scientific problem or an economic problem. The science was done. The manufacturing capacity exists. The gap, when it closes this fast, closes because of unglamorous institutional design. Because someone decided that WHO representatives should be in the EU-M4all room, because someone decided that unredacted assessment reports should flow from the EMA to national regulators via a formal procedure, because someone revised a guidance document in March 2025 to enable a pathway that hadn’t existed before.

None of this is visible from the outside. None of it makes headlines. All of it is what makes 12 days possible.18

Enlli McAleese is a researcher and advisor focused on strengthening medicines regulatory systems in Africa. She previously served as Regulatory Director at 1Day Sooner and worked on the COVID-19 vaccine rollout at the UK Department of Health and Social Care.

In September 2025, Gilead announced a partnership with PEPFAR to procure and distribute lenacapavir to up to 2 million people in low- and middle-income countries.
