item.title: Why there aren’t enough doctors
item.description: A story of regulatory capture.
item.content:encoded:
By Ahmed Ahmed

In September of 1900, Abraham Jacobi, a German emigre whose medical activism made him a prominent figure in the States, made note of a peculiarity of American medicine: The United States boasted far more practicing physicians than the countries in Europe.

Per capita, the United States had twice as many physicians as Great Britain, four times as many as France, five times as many as Germany, six times as many as Italy, and 14 times as many as Russia. Modern data that those in 1900 weren’t fortuitous enough to access make this gap even more curious, as the disparities in wealth and living standards were not large enough to account for the gap in the number of doctors.

A century and a quarter later, the script has entirely flipped and the doctor gap has reversed. The United Kingdom and France have 20% more practicing physicians per capita than the United States and that number increases to 50% and 66% when looking at Italy and Germany, respectively. We are currently in the midst of a physician shortage that is only set to become worse.

The story of America’s relative pittance of physicians shows how prudent policies can transform into regulatory capture.

Origins in the Progressive Era

It would be hard to exaggerate just how lacking medical regulations were in the 1880s, especially as compared to European countries. As one chronicler of the age put it, states “were unwilling to enact laws which would have seriously deterred unlicensed practitioners…the penalties for unlicensed practice were generally nonexistent or insignificant.”1 This Wild West style of medical regulation allowed for all sorts of quack “cures” to endanger public health, from rabid dog saliva to mixtures containing insufficiently diluted deadly poisons.

Progressive Era reformers made it their mission to raise the standards for medical practice. In addition to banning “medicines” that were dangerous, legislatures implemented new requirements to improve public health. Between the 1890s and 1920s, states enacted reforms shutting down diploma mill medical schools and requiring practicing physicians to actually have licenses.

There was good reason for reformers to seek these changes — as Americans moved from rural communities to big cities during this period, they could no longer rely on doctors they knew personally and now had to choose one of many doctors advertising their services. In this more impersonal world, it became difficult to figure out which physicians were actually worthy of trust (and money).

In large part because of these laws, the number of practicing physicians per capita declined by almost a quarter in 20 years. This number would stabilize as those who sought to enter the medical profession began to recognize the value (or at least the practical necessity) of proper credentials.

It also taught a lesson to the medical societies, the groups formed with a primary purpose of advocating for already established doctors. After groups like the American Medical Association succeeded in pushing for licensing reforms and heightening standards for medical schools, they learned just how much power they had in getting legislators to restrict the supply of physicians. Their sway, in no small part earned by the justified trust that Americans have in their doctors, has only grown since the Age of Reform.

The Balanced Budget Act of 1997

By the 1950s, America’s rate of physicians per capita had fallen back down to Earth — in fact, policymakers, fearing a shortage of physicians, would soon work to substantially expand access to medical school and permit a greater number of foreign-trained doctors into the U.S. This was so successful that just three decades later, the opposite fear took hold of those studying healthcare policy: a supposed excess of practicing physicians. A May 1997 New York Times headline captured the zeitgeist well: “Doctors Assert There Are Too Many of Them.”

Policymakers, scholars, and especially groups representing doctors and doctors-to-be asserted that this was a problem for multiple reasons. One was that physicians with more free hours would have a higher willingness to recommend procedures that patients don’t need, wasting their time and potentially jeopardizing their health. Another was that because so many doctors receive payments from the government, a physician surplus would come at a considerable cost to taxpayers. Many were worried that the number of specialists — who made up a larger share of doctors in the U.S. than in other developed nations — would exacerbate these problems, as they had access to expensive and high-margin operations that they’d be especially incentivized to recommend.

In 1997, Congress passed the Balanced Budget Act, the most important law to contemporary discussions of medical regulatory capture. The 1997 law, which primarily aimed to reduce the budget deficit by curtailing the amount of money spent on providers, also sought to eliminate the supposed excess of practicing physicians.

Title IV, Subtitle G, Chapter 2 placed a strict cap on the number of residency slots that were funded by Medicare. Originally, Medicare funding for residency slots was open-ended but, with support from the American Medical Association, the law indefinitely froze the number of residency slots that each hospital could receive money for.

This both reduced the federal financial burden, a major sticking point for the Clinton Administration, and made it much harder for medical school graduates to become physicians. As of just a couple of years ago, only about 116,000 of about 160,000 full-time-equivalent resident positions receive funding from Medicare, with many of the rest relying on states, hospitals, and philanthropic organizations.

The effects have been deleterious, to say the least. Although the number of physicians in the U.S has been increasing per capita, it has not kept up once you account for America’s aging and the fact that older patients require more care than their younger counterparts. Because of the relative shrinking of America’s working-age population, the increased number of seniors means we’re on track for a physician shortage of over 140,000 by 2038. While it’s unreasonable to say this funding change is completely responsible for the doctor shortage, it has not helped.

A critic might argue, reasonably, that we shouldn't simply assume that more funding for residency slots will actually translate to more medical school graduates attaining residencies — there could very well be bottlenecks unrelated to financial causes. While this is of course true, there should be little doubt about the role the Medicare cap plays in limiting the number of residencies. For instance, one study found that under an Affordable Care Act reform that expanded the number of funded residencies in certain hospitals, a one-slot increase in the number of funded slots was associated with 1.3 additional resident FTEs trained.

These exemptions to the residency cap have not appeared to make anyone in the medical establishment upset. In fact, virtually every organization that fought so tirelessly to limit the number of physicians in the 1990s has U-turned, throwing their support behind bipartisan legislative pushes to fix the problem. While the physician shortage remains a cautionary tale of regulatory capture, the current crisis is more one of legislative inertia.

Expanding coverage and the physician bottleneck

The physician shortage is bad on its own, but it’s a major problem for any initiative that seeks to expand health coverage in the U.S.

Although the U.S. has significantly fewer physicians per capita than most of our developed peers, the average physician in the States also has far fewer consultations with patients than doctors in most other advanced economies. One reason for this discrepancy is that America does not have universal healthcare coverage2. Evidence from public health insurance programs in America supports this, too: When those without health insurance receive it, they are much likelier to go to the doctor and when those without face higher co-pays, they are much less likely.

The cost barriers to medical access are a moral travesty and an economic boondoggle. One of the top priorities for policymakers should be addressing the rate of uninsurance, especially in states that didn’t expand Medicaid. Any initiative to further expand healthcare access — whether through existing programs like Medicaid or new programs like one covering all children — needs to figure out how to increase the supply of healthcare providers to make sure that more patients aren’t competing for the same amount of slots offered by physicians. In addition to being bad of its own accord, such a situation risks blowback from the medical establishment if doctors are inundated with more patients without enjoying higher pay.

When faced with an impending shortage in the 1950s, the response was to ramp up the number of medical graduates. Now that we face the same problem and one of the best resposes is to ramp up the opportunities for medical graduates to become residents. Eliminating the cap on Medicare-funded residency slots won’t solve all of the bottleneck problems in healthcare, but it’s a respectable start.

Ahmed Ahmed is a freelance writer and University of Chicago alum.

1

William G. Rothstein, American Physicians in the Nineteenth Century: From Sects to Science (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 1992).

2

Approximately 10% of adults under 65 do not have any form of health insurance — and for those with health insurance, cost sharing is significantly less generous than most public insurance programs in other developed countries.

item.title: Ken Liu and Ada Palmer on constructive visions of the future
item.description: Two science fiction authors try to describe the good life.
item.content:encoded:
This article originally appeared in Issue 16: Flourishing. Subscribe to the print magazine to get future issues delivered to your door.

By Beatrice Erkers

Ada Palmer is a science fiction writer and historian. She teaches early modern European history at the University of Chicago, and her Terra Ignota quartet, beginning with Too Like the Lightning, imagines the world of the 25th century. Ken Liu is an award-winning science fiction and fantasy writer, the author of the Dandelion Dynasty series and The Paper Menagerie and Other Stories, and most recently the author of All That We See or Seem, the first novel in his new series.

I direct the Existential Hope program at Foresight Institute, where we work on circulating more constructive visions of the future. I wanted to know what two people who build worlds for a living think human flourishing would actually look like, and why our imaginations keep sliding toward empire and catastrophe instead. They ended up talking about work far more than I had expected, and about the assumptions underneath it, some of them 2000 years old. I also left with a new term I plan to spread: the Etsy economy.

This interview has been edited for clarity and includes follow-up questions from Asterisk editor in chief Clara Collier.

Permanent crisis

Beatrice Erkers: There’s a trend right now in Silicon Valley of reaching for historical analogies, especially the Renaissance and the age of empires. Why those periods, and why now?

Ada Palmer: Right now, everybody feels like the world is in a state of crisis, and when the world is in a state of crisis, we tend to look at other time periods, both past ones and imagined future ones. You see enormous interest in both past and future during and after the French Revolution, when everyone is suddenly wearing clothing that’s a reproduction of what they imagine ancient Rome looked like. You see the same in the Renaissance, which is also a period of crisis, in the aftermath of the Black Death. History is a wide palette of alternatives that people reach for as a tool to help them understand our world in times of crisis.

The narrower answer is that the periods tech people keep invoking are the ones we associate with disruptive technology. When we talk about the Renaissance, we usually attribute its growth to technology. Tech people love to compare what’s happening now to a Gutenberg revolution. They love to think that a new technology they’re creating is going to accelerate historical change. Just as the Middle Ages were supposedly stagnant and then we suddenly had a period of acceleration toward modernity, they imagine we’re in a period of acceleration toward an exciting science fictional future that’s just around the corner. And the 19th century, another age of empire, is the other age we strongly associate with technology, via the Industrial Revolution.

There’s also the fiction problem. We have an awful lot of science fiction and fantasy about empire, because empire is easy to write about. The power is in the hands of a few characters. It’s very big, but it’s also very dramatic. It’s much harder to write fiction about a complicated plural republic with 52 interlaced political offices and everybody coming from complicated, slightly middle-class backgrounds. Just try writing fiction about the European Union and you will figure this out. So when people look back to history dominated by technology, and forward to futures dominated by technology, they’re seeing a lot of models of empire.

We have an awful lot of science fiction and fantasy about empire, because empire is easy to write about. The power is in the hands of a few characters. It’s much harder to write fiction about a complicated plural republic with 52 interlaced political offices and everybody coming from complicated, slightly middle-class backgrounds.

Ken Liu: I agree with all that, and I’d add that there’s an element of justification going on. When history is invoked, it’s often a way to explain and legitimate exercises of power. When Venice was trying to become a great city, it went to Alexandria to steal the body of St. Mark, so that it could prove itself a great Christian city. When people think they’re making great transformations, it can seem a little scary, and one way to legitimate it is to say: Historically, things happen because they’re inevitable. You can complain about what I’m doing all you want, but I’m just an agent of history.

Ada: We’re all aware of the type of history we call Great Man theory of history, which centers all agency in a couple of heroized figures, and which we’ve been trying to move away from. But one of the biggest types of history people turn to instead is Great Forces history, in which everything is giant gears grinding, and as soon as there’s a certain amount of torque in the system, the machine tips. That’s an important analytical tool. But just as much as Great Man history, Great Forces history erases agency for everyone, except perhaps economists, who get to believe they’re wielding the great forces.

Ken: That’s my favorite version: Economics as storytelling with numbers.

Ada: And if you don’t have a choice in the thing you’re doing, if it’s an inevitability, that’s one of many ways to accept it and justify it, both to others and to yourself.

Beatrice: How much of this is really about AI, though? That’s the revolution Silicon Valley believes it’s living through.

Ada: I think we’re wrong to separate generative AI and call it a completely new revolution. I often talk to Silicon Valley people who want to ask, are we so special that we’ve had six Gutenberg revolutions in a row, 10 years apart? And I say no, we’re having one Gutenberg revolution: the computer.

The personal computer, the internet, the cell phone, social media, and generative AI are all iterations of the same one fundamental technological change, the same way Gutenberg’s press kept having new impacts for decades through news networks, pamphlets, and eventually the newspaper. A little too much of our analysis of Silicon Valley right now is of the past five years instead of the past 20.

The guy behind the refrigerator

Beatrice: Ada, when I interviewed you before, you mentioned that Petrarch could imagine political change but not the end of disease. And what happened instead is that we ended a lot of diseases. What’s our version of that blind spot?

Ada: He thought it would be easier to defeat the Dire Horseman War than the Dire Horseman Plague. And we’ve found that in fact we’ve made more progress against the Dire Horseman Plague than against the Dire Horseman War. Some of the STEM problems have proved easier than some of the social science problems.

We’re not entirely missing this, but you constantly hear people encouraging STEM, STEM, STEM while diminishing the humanities and the social sciences as partners, whereas people who are really deep in it, who are scientists, understand there’s a symbiosis: We don’t make progress by funding just one of the three. There’s a perception that wealth flows toward technological innovation, rather than recognizing that wealth flows toward lots of kinds of innovation, only some of which is technological.

Ken: I don’t want to focus so much on Silicon Valley, though. The problems we have today don’t stem from a few people or a few inventions. They have their roots much further back, in what I’d call the gradual mechanization of humans.

Take AI displacing jobs. This is not something that happened in the last five years. We’ve been creating the conditions for it for a century or more. If you worked in customer service 40 years ago, you were a respected professional. Over time we turned those into scripted jobs. Once you’ve gotten things to that point, it’s not very difficult to throw the human out and put in a language model. It’s not the model that caused this. It’s that we’ve been making humans behave more and more like machines, up and down the chain: devaluing work, taking the meaning out of it, turning it into a mechanistic process where you’re a cog performing what your role demands. The pushback Silicon Valley is getting now is the tip of the iceberg. What’s really being expressed is a much deeper loss of meaning, dignity, and participation.

Ada: I’ve been using a simile lately for when people say generative AI is causing problem X, when we’ve been talking about problem X since before the 1980s.

You’ve filled your refrigerator for the first time with something weird, synthetic meat, say, and the refrigerator is straining. Meanwhile there’s a guy behind the refrigerator hitting it with a sledgehammer, and he’s been hitting it for weeks. But somehow everyone’s blaming the new substance rather than the fact that there is a guy actively dismantling the refrigerator from behind. There have been active dismantlings of worker strength, solidarity, unions, skill, and employee rights, systematically, for decades longer than generative AI has existed.

The Etsy economy

Beatrice: So what should we be moving toward? What does a flourishing direction actually look like?

Ken: We should not be thinking about this in terms of preserving the status quo against disruption from AI, because the status quo is terrible. We should be thinking much harder about how to restore meaning to people’s lives.

In the last few generations, most of us have become used to tying our identity to our employment. When we fight to preserve jobs, we’re treating a job as two things at once: an economic means of support and a source of meaning. We need to separate them, and think about how people find meaning outside gainful employment: from connection with other people, from a sense of control, from a sense that we make a difference.

Why do so many people repeat, as though it were proven, that not all of us can be artists, singers, poets? Says who? Surely there are ways for all of us to live a life of meaning without being employed or paid for it.

Ada: This is something I think about a lot. Classic science fiction that engaged with the future of automation kept producing the same few visions. In the ‘60s and ‘70s, quite a few writers advanced the thesis that if mankind didn’t have to work, everyone would commit mass suicide: Work was the only thing keeping humanity from self-destruction. There’s the vision of the machines rising up, the Frankensteinian robot, The Matrix. And there’s the vision of humans living in paradise domes making art and philosophy all day while robots do everything else. Notice that last one assumes that, liberated from work, humans will only want to do very elite, high-status activities. Art and philosophy, not gardening and taking care of injured bats.

But look at our present: There are so many meaningful vocations people would love to do and don’t, because meaningful vocations are economically exploited. We don’t pay teachers. We don’t pay people who do social work, or care for the environment, or rehabilitate injured seagulls. We don’t pay our artists and actors much, except a very few. A lot of people, given a steady paycheck to live on, would much rather work at the bat sanctuary.

Another future I enjoy playing with is: What if the future is the Etsy economy, where we all make beautiful handcrafted bespoke things and buy them from each other? Maybe you enjoy drawing pterodactyls, maybe crochet. Everybody enjoys making and doing things. A future where we all make and do things and purchase them from each other is a beautiful future.

Ken: That’s my low-art future. Not everybody has to become a bestseller. You can make things for a few people, and that can be very satisfying. Or the future in which staying home with your kids as a dad is a perfectly respectable, meaningful thing to do. If you want to stay home and teach your kids and play games, why the heck not, as long as you find meaning in it.

Ada: And if anyone says that doesn’t contribute to humanity: You’ve raised kids, and they’re going to go contribute to humanity. We know good, supportive parenting produces happier, more creative, more generative kids. But it’s another kind of labor we devalue, partly because it’s historically coded female, like childcare, elder care, and teaching generally. If we simply make sure everyone can have a living no matter what they do, a lot of people have things they would love to go do.

Ken: Decouple remuneration from the status of the work you do, and things will look very different.

Ada: And we have study after study confirming that when we run universal basic income experiments, this is what happens. Everyone’s afraid people will be lazy, and instead people are energized. They start businesses they’d long dreamed of, open the café, start producing art, start taking care of the town square.

There are surprisingly many win-win investments a society can make that we don’t make, because we’ve trained people toward zero-sum thinking about both business and politics. When you show them something where the investment makes people happy and boosts the economy and pays for itself, they just feel suspicious. Too good to be true.

Ken: There’s a reason so much ’60s science fiction has as its central theme the idea that humans must be made to struggle for humanity to move forward. There are tons of Star Trek episodes dedicated to the idea that being taken care of by your machines is actually a prison, and you must be put back into a position of struggle. That attitude came of age during the Cold War, and there are ideological reasons it was being pushed. We don’t have to accept it as the only way to imagine the future.

Clara Collier: A world where humans are free to make art, study, care for injured seagulls, and so on, assumes a very high degree of automation of all the less pleasant tasks that exist in the economy, including ones that are quite difficult and involved. I’d love to tie that back to the conversation about AI and the devaluation of human labor. How do both of you think of the challenge of creating a world where humans aren’t needed to do all the grunt work of civilization, but still have real power?

Ken: Our fear is not giving up power to AI (you can no more give up power to AI than you can give up power to your refrigerator), but ceding power to those who build and control AI. It’s the same with every technological transformation: The real problem is almost never the machine itself, but those behind the machine. This is not a new problem. We’ve been dealing with the concentration of power and the corrupting effects of the few deciding the fate of all for practically the entirety of our history. The answer is always the same: Devolve power to the individual, constrain the power of states to monopolize knowledge, build social technologies for collective decision-making that will prevent the few from controlling everything.

We’ve been dealing with the concentration of power and the corrupting effects of the few deciding the fate of all for practically the entirety of our history. The answer is always the same.

Ada: Another way to think about it is that this wouldn’t be a big change, just a continuation of a millennia-long trend. Since the earliest days of tool use, human civilization has been a long process of humans finding ways to do less grunt work, to have more time for leisure, comfortable living, and more pleasurable work like making art. Computers, printers, washing machines, bicycles, motors, horses, the wheel — they all let us do less grunt work, and did not reduce our power. The only things that reduce our power are institutional changes, government, disempowering labor. It’s another instance of “Policy is everything.”

Two categories of people

Beatrice: So how do we make the win-win argument actually stick?

Ada: One interesting approach is to notice that the fear is really two separate assumptions. A: There are lots of people who, if they didn’t have to work, wouldn’t work. B: If there were a bunch of people around who weren’t working, that would somehow be harmful.

And B goes way, way back. I was just rereading the beginning of Machiavelli’s Discourses, where he agrees with Livy that if you want a thriving country, you need to found it somewhere with constant difficulty, to keep the popular classes busy and striving. Because otherwise there will be indolence, and indolence will make the populace foolish and manipulable. We’re fighting a 2,000-year-old assumption that people comfortably living without hard work will somehow be harmful.

Ken: I do want to point out one possible pushback against this position. There will be a percentage of the population who derive their happiness primarily from having higher status than others. The question is how numerous they really are, and whether their unhappiness would make the system not work. I don’t think that’s clear. But let’s not presumptively say the vision is impossible because some people won’t like it.

Ada: It’s worth zooming in on people’s emotional investment in inequality. The person who fears that if people don’t have to work, lots of people won’t work, and that this would be terrible, is generally speaking perfectly happy reading 19th-century novels about the aristocratic class, all of whom have inherited wealth, do nothing, and have Regency balls.

What that semi-hypocrisy reveals is an assumption that there are two categories of people: one that can be trusted with leisure, and another that becomes harmful and destructive given leisure. And that goes back to a much deeper assumption running through huge swathes of history: that there is a category of person that knows how to rule, and a much larger portion of the population that cannot understand power.

[There is] a much deeper assumption running through huge swathes of history: that there is a category of person that knows how to rule, and a much larger portion of the population that cannot understand power.

Humanity keeps reinventing aristocracy with new justifications. A lot of what Silicon Valley calls meritocracy right now is exactly this, and it is fundamentally undemocratic.

The PowerPoints are the problem

Beatrice: We’ve been circling AI this whole conversation. What does the discourse around it get wrong, and what is it actually good for?

Ken: I’m frustrated with the conversation around AI largely because the things we focus on, such as the loss of jobs (which have already been drained of humanity and meaning) and the use of copyrighted materials (as if copyright were an adequate proxy for our dignity or non-economic rights), are so uninteresting. Many of the negative effects we attribute to the AI revolution are really the result of how we’ve chosen to dehumanize labor and reward capital, and AI is nothing more than a symptom of much deeper root problems. The questions I find more interesting: If this technology is supposedly so powerful, why should it be controlled by a few companies, and the few governments in charge of those companies? Concentration of control is the much bigger problem. Labels like “pro-AI” or “anti-AI” are meaningless — we should all be pro-human, and we should all be leery of humans who would try to use technology to control other humans.

And if we’re talking about flourishing, look at what these technologies can actually do. So much of the supposed productivity from AI is about writing emails and generating PowerPoint slides, workers using tokens to decompose PowerPoint slides into Markdown text. Absolutely useless stuff.

The real benefit, and I believe there is one, is in scientific research. These machines are capable of cognitive tasks that used to be extremely costly: folding proteins, proving new theorems, exploring large state spaces of chemical possibilities. Go talk to working scientists. They will tell you AI has genuinely transformed the way they work. I wish more of the conversation focused on that. AI will not transform our lives in a positive way by writing our office emails.

Clara: I’m curious to discuss this more, because of Asterisk’s audience. We have many readers who are software engineers or work in other technical fields, and for them, AI has absolutely transformed their work. Conversely, I hear a lot of scientists these days complaining about how AI labs are overselling the benefits, especially in biomedical research.

Ken: Like any technology, AI’s ultimate impact has to be worked out by each individual scientist, artist, student, doctor, lawyer, etc. In the same way that the internet, after the bursting of the bubble, transformed our lives in ways none of the pioneers had envisioned, AI is going to do the same — the bubble will burst, and then we’ll see, in 10 years, that the true impact will be nothing like what we are predicting now. The cognitive boost from AI will not be useful for some tasks, but it will be incredibly useful for many other tasks. It takes time, creativity, and experimentation before individual humans can figure out how this technology can (or cannot) transform their work in meaningful ways. And once again, in order for this sort of creativity and experimentation to be possible, AI must evolve in ways that allow individual data sovereignty and leave control in the hands of users, not in the hands of a few large companies and their state patrons.

Ada: Here I really like Cory Doctorow’s terms centaur and reverse centaur, and I think they do a great job describing why some people are finding generative AI very helpful and others are finding it loathsome. Here centaur means when the human is on top supported by the machine, helped to do more, and that’s what a lot of scientists using machine learning or programmers using coding tools are finding, the tool helps them do more as the horse part lets a centaur run faster. A reverse centaur is when the human is in the loop to support the machine, like when people are tasked to correct LLM-generated material, or run errands to the machine’s direction; the horse is on top with the human running at the bottom. What we keep finding is that people using generative AI in a centaur mode often like it, while those who have miserable experiences tend to be those put in the reverse centaur position. Cory has a great book analyzing this more.

I’ll also add another arena where generative AI is useful: small-scale bespoke tasks where there’s no budget. I saw a really good use of an LLM where the city of Bowling Green, Kentucky, gave a huge survey to every citizen, got about 8,000 responses back, and had the LLM sort them. Their office with its tiny staff could never have gone through those themselves. It let them discover that the top two issues in town were funding for the English-as-a-second-language program and one intersection with bad traffic, neither of which was on any politician’s radar. Masses of information sorted on a small scale to solve a social science problem.

And here’s a middle-ground model I’ve been enjoying, from a comparison someone made on Bluesky. We keep talking as if the two possible futures are that generative AI transforms everything, or the bubble pops and it vanishes. But consider the trajectory of radioactive material. We discovered radium and uranium, and we were so excited. We put them in power plants, in weapons, in face cream, in cough syrup, in wristwatches. Well, 90% of what we put them in turned out to kill us, so we dialed it back by 90%. But the 10% where it was really useful, we still use, and all of us benefit from it every day: power, medicine, space systems.

90% of what we put [radium and uranium into] turned out to kill us. But the 10% where it was really useful, we still use, and all of us benefit from it every day: power, medicine, space systems. I can imagine that future for generative AI.

I can imagine that future for generative AI. It’s really bad as a therapist, really bad as a teacher substitute, and PowerPoint is bad for all humans. But it’s really good at sorting survey responses and folding proteins, so we keep those. That’s not a middle ground I hear people talk about much. Like any technology: We try it in a bunch of ways, we find what it’s great at, and then we use it for the things it’s great at.

Despair is how we lose

Beatrice: Does it matter how we imagine futures? Dystopian visions are certainly the more widespread and available ones right now.

Ada: What’s harmful is when our visions of the future are homogeneous and unquestioned, whichever direction they point. That’s true of Golden Age science fiction unquestioningly assuming an inexorable historical arc toward a Western-dominated, imperial future for humanity. And it’s true of the glut of dystopian and apocalyptic fiction that started just after the year 2000, a decade and a half before things started to feel bad in real life to most people.

When I first came to the University of Chicago, I had lunch with a colleague in creative writing and asked what fraction of the students were writing science fiction or fantasy. He said: We only have two students in the major who aren’t writing dystopia. That’s how saturated the consensus was. And when you get consensus about the future people stop thinking about the fact that we have agency. A lot of people say: We know the future is going to suck, so why bother doing anything? But despair is how we lose.

Ken: Beyond homogeneity of vision being bad, homogeneity of interpretation is bad too. Interesting portrayals of the future function like mythologies, or dreams. They’re open to interpretation. Writing science fiction as a philosophical blueprint for how to construct society is a valid mode, but it’s not the only one. And a lot of the most powerful science fiction is mythological, a thought experiment that opens up possibilities rather than a literal prediction. If I were to portray the Etsy arts-and-crafts future Ada described, I would not write it as everyone happy, like lotus-eaters. I’d try to imagine why the vision is compelling for some people and why some would find it dystopic, and find the human story in it. By portraying that emotional dream, readers can find their own path through it and figure out whether the vision speaks to them.

There’s a reason so many wonderful works of imaginative literature can be read multiple ways. Take Susanna Clarke’s Piranesi: Some readers finish it finding that world incredibly beautiful, and some don’t, but you will have an emotional reaction you then have to explain to yourself. That’s where the power of this kind of imagination comes from.

Beyond homogeneity of vision being bad, homogeneity of interpretation is bad too. Interesting portrayals of the future [are] open to interpretation….By portraying that emotional dream, readers can find their own path through it and figure out whether the vision speaks to them.

Ada: That’s one of the most valuable things about not just imagining a future but having a storyteller actually sit down and tell a story in it: You explore the premise in its messiness, working and not working, for the people it works for and the people it doesn’t. I hang out with a lot of people involved in fixing democracy, and they’ll have a great idea, say sortition, choosing officials by lottery instead of voting, and sortition will work perfectly.

The reason they think so is that their sortition exists in a perfect abstract world, and they’re comparing it to American democracy, which has existed for 250 years, during which everyone has had an incentive to hack it. Of course perfect sortition looks better than imperfect voting. What a science fiction writer, or a historian, can do is show you sortition in action: working, being corrupted, working for these people and not those. Then you’re comparing the imaginary-and-flawed to the real-and-flawed, which puts them on par. That’s why science fiction is so good at helping us spot the weaknesses, the people left behind, and the “we could use this badly, guys” problems of innovations before we get to them. We don’t just depict the world, we tell a story in it, with conflicts and failures.

Beatrice: Do you each have a favorite element from your own worldbuilding that you’d like to see in our toolbox in terms of creating a more flourishing world?

Ken: Imagine a future in which we run our AI on our own hardware, our own little boxes, open source, open weights, with total control over what data and what access to our lives we give it. In that future, your personal AI becomes part of your extended cognition. In my novel, the main character, Julia, has an AI like this and uses it essentially as a mirror. She uses it to examine her own actions, figure out where she went wrong, what she’s doing well, and how to amplify her abilities. In the same way that writing allowed humans to reflect on our own cognition and think deeper thoughts, a personal AI would be cognitively transformative.

Ada: Besides better transit, so we can all see our friends more often, in Terra Ignota I imagine work divided into two categories. There are “voker” jobs, from vocateur, vocation: a job you do because you feel called to it, because you love it, a passion project. And there are the jobs somebody has to do. Somebody has to repair the robots that repair the other robots when they get into a state that requires human ingenuity. In our society we don’t differentiate these, even though they operate completely differently and we reward them completely differently. In this imagined future, your identity is not your job unless you love your job. Notably, this requires no technological change at all. It’s just a change in how we think about work.

Beatrice: Last question. Thinking big for what is possible in the future: What’s your existential hope vision, the thing we should be aiming toward?

Ada: Poverty and educational access. We have all these studies confirming that when people are desperate, worried every day about where tomorrow’s meal is coming from, it takes a huge cognitive load. The vast majority of computing power on Earth is human brains, and a huge amount of it is dedicated to worrying about where lunch is coming from tomorrow. If you want to free up computing power, solve poverty.

Ken: I like that answer a lot, but I’ll go in a slightly different direction. In a lot of far-future science fiction, humans or aliens build some amazing computing machine that harnesses a black hole, and somehow all that computing power is devoted to militaristic ends: how to kill, how to defend, how to conquer the universe so no one else can take it over. I find that incredibly sad, and not realistic. Look at the computing power on the planet today, human brains: I don’t think the vast majority of it is devoted to destroying our enemies. A huge amount of our energy goes to questions like: How do I become a better person? How do I love my friend more? How do I get closer to ultimate reality, and why do we exist? We devote enormous computing power to contemplative questions, to matters beyond materialism. I’d love to see us engage more with that side of ourselves: exploring consciousness, engaging with what Hinduism has to say about what consciousness is, with Daoism, with esoteric philosophies, with meditation. Things that have nothing to do with the day-to-day struggle to survive, and everything to do with ultimate reality. I don’t want people to forget that’s part of human flourishing too.

item.title: How Chinese companies talk about recursive self-improvement
item.description: RSI with Chinese characteristics.
item.content:encoded:
By Zilan Qian

“The United States is racing forward broadly, in part because it is worried about what happens if China gets to self-improving AI first ” — Ezra Klein, The New York Times

Recursive self-improvement, broadly understood as an AI system iteratively designing an increasingly capable successor without much extra input from humans, is widely regarded as a focal point in the U.S.-China AI competition. As Matt Sheehan from the Carnegie Endowment has argued, parts of the U.S. research community see RSI as a way to lock in a lasting geopolitical lead.

China has not turned a blind eye. The Chinese government picked up the term in its recent top policy document, “AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0,” and almost all Chinese AI companies have become increasingly vocal about RSI and related ideas this year.

It seems, thus, that RSI is indeed the goal that both sides are racing towards. But the reality is not so simple. For one, we don’t understand what Chinese companies mean when they talk about AI research automation or RSI — even as more and more of them adopt the term.

Chinese companies already disclose a good deal about how they use AI in their research, sometimes in more detail than U.S. labs. Based on this analysis, we argue that RSI in China, so far, looks less like a state-led race than a bottom-up, commercial trend. We suggest that the U.S. and China AI researchers should start by building a shared vocabulary and comparable transparency about how AI is used to build AI.

The many faces of RSI in China

RSI is a confusing term even in Silicon Valley, where it is used to describe everything from AI automating parts of AI research to an uncontrollable intelligence explosion. Similarly, it means many things in China — but not necessarily the same ones. Just last year, Chinese companies discussed related ideas using varied phrases such as “self-evolution (自我进化/自进化),” “self-iteration (自我迭代),” and “self-training (自我训练).” As the table below shows, pulling from releases from firms1, even the same firm does not always use the same term.

The term RSI (递归式自我改进) has only entered Chinese companies’ vocabulary in the past few months. The shift is evident at companies like Alibaba. In 2025, CEO Eddie Wu said AI would achieve “self-learning” (自主学习). It would be able to build its own training infrastructure, optimize data pipelines and upgrade model architectures, which would eventually lead to a singularity: “Once a certain singularity is crossed, human society will be as if it pressed the accelerate button, and the speed of technological progress will exceed our imagination.” He did not use the term RSI.

In September 2026, he did use the word, defining it as the point when “the model discovers its shortcomings from real-world feedback, designs experiments, constructs data, and evaluates results, thus driving its own evolution in a continuous cycle.” The new definition focuses on the feedback loop and does not emphasize the acceleration of progress, which is a narrower but also more concrete ambition than his 2025 vision.

Z.ai founder Tang Jie’s wording followed a similar path. In a May 2026 post on X, he called “self-evolution” a “promising path.” In July, he described “self-evolving” (自我进化) as “AI training AI” with models writing their own code, cleaning and synthesizing their own data, and training themselves. In a September interview with Qiushi, the Party’s flagship theory journal, he picked up the term RSI, though he called it “recursive super intelligence,” likely mixing up what the acronym stands for. He argued that if models could continuously improve and correct themselves, they might soon reach a singularity and surpass human intelligence, though they could also plateau.

The same thing happened for Xiaomi. In March 2026, Luo Fuli, head of Xiaomi’s MiMo models, named “self-evolution” (自进化) the most important development for AGI in the coming year. She described it as an agent framework with verifiable constraints and a loop that keeps the model iterating toward a goal. Xiaomi’s later MiMo-V2.6 technical report instead adopts “recursive self-improvement (RSI),” defined as models that “expand their capabilities through sustained exploration and feedback.”

Note: Each marker is one saved company document (release note, blog post, paper, model card, filing, or a founder or executive statement reported by media) that contains the term, placed at its publication date; Chinese and English spellings are pooled except for RSI, which is split by language. Corpora cover each firm’s model-lab channels from July 1, 2025 to October 10, 2026 (Alibaba 286 documents, ByteDance 249, Baidu 226, MiniMax 183, Xiaomi 164, DeepSeek 122, Z.ai 105, Moonshot 102).

Across all three examples, the idea of AI improving AI took shape before the terminology of RSI being adopted. Chinese companies have only been using “RSI” since July 2026. But what Chinese AI companies talk about regarding RSI does not appear too different from what they talk about regarding self-evolution or self-learning. Using AI for AI research is thus a long-standing practice with many loosely defined and often interchangeable labels, of which “RSI” is the newest.

Unlike in Silicon Valley, where the two concepts are closely linked, the adoption of “RSI” in China has not brought about much talk of an intelligence explosion. Chinese AI leaders occasionally mention a singularity, as Wu did in 2025’s speech and Tang in his Qiushi interview. However, when they describe where self-improving AI leads, they mostly point to real-world applications. Tang describes a future in which “every sector — security, finance, law, e-commerce — will be reshaped.” Wu envisioned that artificial superintelligence “may create a batch of ‘super scientists’ and ‘full-stack super engineers’” to address “medical challenges, new materials, sustainable energy and climate problems.” DeepSeek’s Liang Wenfeng imagines AI after the singularity to be embodied and “walk into the real world, can do your housework, can care for you in old age.”

Chinese AI companies can push RSI ahead without a settled term for it. However, policymakers cannot.

Why do Chinese companies mention RSI?

In September 2026, a five-hour Saturday salon in Shanghai gathered researchers, well-known investors, financial advisers, and incubators to discuss RSI. It was organized by HongShan, formerly Sequoia Capital China, one of the country’s most influential venture capital firms. Key investors have started treating RSI as a theme worth organizing around. In various reports surrounding this event, RSI is described as the field “VCs are chasing.”

Investor appetite may partially explain why Chinese AI companies started using the term. In June 2026, Anthropic published “When AI Builds Itself,” an essay that received heavy media coverage in China. Within a month, Chinese companies began adopting the label. One plausible explanation is commercial. Having seen RSI attract attention and capital in the U.S., Chinese companies may see the concept as a way to raise money themselves.

Indeed, new Chinese startups built around AI research automation, some led by founders with close ties to the U.S. AI research community, have raised substantial funding in the second half of 2026. SuperDen Intelligence (超衍智能), founded by an assistant professor at Tsinghua in June 2026, raised a total of nearly 400 million RMB (60 million USD) in their angel and angel+ round in September. The founder, who worked at Google DeepMind and Microsoft, said that he first had the idea of auto-research at GDM. Similarly, MetaCircle (元环智能), founded in May 2026, raised hundreds of millions RMB in their seed round in the past two months2. The founder is also an assistant professor at Tsinghua, best known for the KAN neural-network architecture, which he developed during his MIT PhD under Max Tegmark.

Z.ai’s recent fundraising shows how RSI as a label may help with raising capital. On September 13, the company announced about USD $5 billion in new financing. Three days later, it told analysts that about 60% of the net proceeds would go to next-generation GLM models and its “Fully Self Training” system. The next day, it published its blog post “Toward Recursive Self-Improvement,” which Chinese tech media reported as “Zhipu’s first RSI result.”

STAR Market Daily, an authoritative financial news outlet specializing in China’s sci-tech capital markets, covered the sequence under the headline “Zhipu bets on the RSI narrative after intensive fundraising.” While the timeline itself does not prove that the company intentionally raised RSI for the sake of fundraising, it suggests the RSI framing was aimed at least partly at investors.

While RSI may serve partly as a marketing strategy, this does not mean Chinese companies are not serious about using AI for AI research. The work is useful in its own right, especially under compute constraints. Investors increasingly care about the compute cost of developing and serving models, and reliance on foreign chips can raise compute costs and add supply risk. Chinese business media reports suggest that investors examine downstream AI application companies’ “computing power procurement structure,” and projects “that rely entirely on overseas high-end A/H100 series chips” may see their valuations “significantly discounted,” or may not even make it to due diligence.

Automating AI research could help relax this bottleneck. Chinese companies have applied AI to infrastructure and kernel work, helping their models run more efficiently on Chinese-made chips. This gives them a reason to keep automating AI research, whatever they call it, and could make them more attractive to investors, even if the research itself needs more compute in the short term.

Overall, it is still hard to distinguish whether Chinese AI companies genuinely believe in RSI, or are just using the term to fundraise. In many cases, one could both genuinely believe in RSI and want to cash in on it — after all, money is necessary to train frontier models, and Chinese companies receive much less investment and revenue than their U.S. counterparts3.

China starts to think about RSI risks

Chinese AI companies can push RSI ahead without a settled term for it. However, policymakers cannot. To intervene, regulators need to know what exactly to intervene on. How RSI enters China’s policy and public debate can therefore signal whether and when China might regulate it, and whether the U.S. and China understand it similarly enough to talk about it.

RSI first appeared in a policy document in September 2026, when TC260, China’s main standard-making body on cyber and AI, released AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0, the most comprehensive official Chinese taxonomy of AI safety risks. Its introduction mentions RSI with a slightly altered literal translation, “自我递归提升” (self-recursive improvement), accompanied by a full mention of “recursive self-improvement” in the official English translation.

Prominently noted in the beginning, however, is that RSI is a future trend to observe rather than an urgent risk to tackle: “More profoundly, AI has demonstrated a self-accelerating trend of model and algorithm autonomous learning, optimization, and recursive self-improvement. Whether the speed and direction of technological evolution may exceed human anticipation and control demands attention and vigilance.” The rest of the document does not come back to RSI when discussing AI safety risks.

While the term has only appeared in one policy document, public discussion around RSI has picked up. In China, emerging discourse — driven by governance or technical researchers and state-affiliated media — now covers warnings of RSI risks linked to ASI (超级人工智能), recommendations on related regulations, and technical research, but with an emphasis on keeping AI progress safe rather than preventing it completely.

On September 30, 2026, Study Times (学习时报), the official newspaper of the party’s highest internal training institute4, published an article by AI governance professor Zeng Yi. The article describes RSI as “a key path to AGI” and “the main trigger point for loss-of-control risk”. It argues that once AI can improve its own architecture, “the positive cycle of intelligence gains could accelerate to the point where humans cannot keep up at all.” While the article warned against the risk of getting humans out of the AI research loop, it equally stressed that one cannot “stop eating for the fear of choking (因噎废食)”. Abandoning the research is not an option, but rather “self-improvement proposals and substantive architectural changes” so that “humans hold final control under any circumstances.”

The public evidence does not support the claim that China is racing to reach RSI first.

An op-ed in the semi-state-linked Economic Observer5 (经济观察报) went further, proposing a detailed framework for governing RSI. It sorts AI into five levels of “recursive capability,” from ordinary research assistance to systems that train and deploy their own successors, with obligations that scale accordingly. The lowest level needs no extra rules beyond existing product-safety and data-protection law, while the highest should never run “without external oversight” and should trigger “international notification.” It describes the danger of superhuman capabilities brought by RSI spanning cyber and military domains. It also proposes four categories — capabilities, resources, evaluation and deployment — and asks that no single recursive system holds research, evaluation, resource and deployment rights at once.

Beyond policy proposals, technical research on RSI safety has also started to appear in academic discourse. A group of researchers from leading Chinese universities and research institutes measured how much of AI research AI already does. They logged 769 tasks from the development of its own agentic research model and found that AI was involved in 96.5% of tasks and proposed most methods, but humans made the final choice in 85.5% of method decisions.

These Chinese researchers also argued that authority over human safety needs to be handled seriously, and each advance in AI capability should be matched by investment in alignment and oversight, with clear rules on whose goals AI pursues and who remains accountable. Similar work is multiplying: The Chinese Academy of Sciences has proposed studying the “evolutionary safety” of recursively self-improving AI; Shanghai AI Lab has explored using RSI itself to improve safety (“recursive safety improvement”) and documented how self-evolving agents “misevolve.”

Overall, the discussion of RSI and its safety in China resembles a bottom-up effort. AI companies, AI governance scholars, and technical safety researchers talk about it most often, while top-level policy is gradually catching up as the topic becomes more prominent in AI discourse. There is little public evidence that the top leadership treats RSI as a priority. But the broader AI community, from AI companies to AI governance scholars and research communities, is becoming more vocal about it, which may inform and influence thinking at the top.

Chinese AI companies disclose details about AI R&D automation

Thinking about RSI risks in China is still at an early stage. However, one basis for governing RSI is already partly in place: disclosure. People need to know what AI is actually doing inside AI labs to set rules. Chinese AI companies have already started to publish about where and how they use AI in their research.

Firstly, they disclose where they apply AI in the research pipeline in order to showcase their models’ automated research capabilities. MiniMax reports that M2.7 is capable of constructing complex Agent Harness on its own. It has also described agents that “help with literature review, track a pre-set experiment spec, pipeline data and other artifacts, and launch experiments” in an RL scenario.

Xiaomi introduced CodeMidas, “an agentic pipeline that turns implemented functionality in existing codebases into executable RL environments using source code as its only task-specific input.” It resulted in “5,545 training tasks from 3,185 open-source codebases spanning 23 programming languages and 15 technical domains.” Z.ai’s “Toward Recursive Self-Improvement” blog post states that its GLM-5.3-powered Infra Agent helped build the inference system that serves GLM-5.3-Flash on more than 100,000 Chinese-made accelerators, chips designed for AI computation.

RSI direction: Firms (linked to examples)

Overall research workflow: MiniMax, ByteDance Seed (Seed for Seed), Alibaba (Iris)
Harness: MiniMax
Training data / RL environments: Xiaomi, DeepSeek, Z.ai, Moonshot, Alibaba (Qwen3), Alibaba (Qwen-UI-Agent), Tencent Hunyuan (using DeepSeek’s model though)
Training / inference infrastructure: Z.ai, Moonshot, MiniMax, ByteDance Seed (CUDA Agent)

They also describe how the AI did the work and what it achieved. According to MiniMax’s announcement in March 2026, MiniMax’s M2.7 ran a loop of more than 100 rounds on an internal harness and reported a 30% gain on an internal evaluation set. In this process, M2.7 studied failed attempts, planned changes, edited the harness code, reran the evaluation, and made decisions on whether to keep the change. Moonshot’s Kimi K3 report (July 2026, revised August) says agents built its training tasks and the starting workspaces for its personal-assistant tasks, and that earlier Kimi models wrote its fine-tuning data.

Z.ai’s blog post in September 2026, “Toward Recursive Self-Improvement,” mentions the division of labor during building infrastructure: “Engineers defined objectives and system boundaries. The agent handled analysis, hypotheses, and code changes. The experimental environment provided layered, timely, and verifiable feedback.” Z.ai says the work, much of which it credits to the agent, tripled end-to-end throughput relative to the initial baseline.

By contrast, OpenAI and Anthropic mostly publish aggregate usage statistics, often oriented toward risk assessment. Anthropic says Claude wrote more than 80% of the code it merged (May 2026), and “leads” 26% of its AI R&D work (August 2026). OpenAI does break agents’ output down by research task, but only as token counts.

Of course, OpenAI and Anthropic also sometimes report more details. For example, OpenAI’s blog post introducing GPT-5.5 this April says Codex analyzed weeks of production traffic and wrote new load-balancing rules for serving, which made token generation over 20% faster. Anthropic has mentioned that in an experiment, Claude Sonnet 5 spent 60 hours trying to fix alignment failures in an early checkpoint of Claude Opus 4.8 by creating training data.

But overall, in our assessment, Chinese AI companies seem to be a bit more detailed about AI R&D automation applications. Part of this contrast comes from the fact that Chinese AI companies are more open and thus publish more technical reports reporting the AI’s process step by step.

Policy implications

Our findings suggest that RSI in China, so far, looks less like a state-led geopolitical race than a bottom-up, commercially driven trend.

First, Chinese companies do not even share a language for it. They picked up “RSI” only recently, largely following discussions in Silicon Valley, and still use the term to mean different things. Second, one visible driver is commercial: RSI helps with fundraising, aims at easing compute constraints in the future, and shows investors efficiency gains.. Third, RSI barely features in policy. Its only appearance in an official document treats it as a trend to watch with “vigilance,” and prominent voices in party-affiliated media emphasize keeping it under human control. Fourth, Chinese companies already disclose some details about how they use AI in research, which gives outside observers more to work with than the race narrative suggests.

The public evidence does not support the claim that China is racing to reach RSI first. Commercial incentives and competitive market dynamics can encourage Chinese AI companies to double down on research automation without explicit policy instruction or geopolitical racing dynamics. Therefore, regardless of geopolitical calculations, the world must prepare for a scenario in which automation of AI research happens more aggressively in leading AI labs in both countries.

One should therefore focus on understanding the capabilities being developed in leading labs in both countries. Before pursuing ambitious international agreements, researchers, companies, and policymakers could take two basic but necessary steps.

First, scientists and AI researchers from both countries could develop a shared vocabulary that distinguishes among the automation of individual research tasks, closed feedback loops, and systems that produce self-sustaining acceleration in capabilities. Exchanges could help establish what each side means by terms such as “automating AI research,” “self-evolution,” and “recursive self-improvement.” Using these terms to describe very different processes obscures the risks involved and makes it harder to identify appropriate safeguards.

Second, companies could adopt common transparency standards. Reports should specify which research tasks AI performs, how its performance is evaluated, how often humans intervene, how much AI accelerates different parts of and overall AI research, what decisions remain under human control, and what safeguards prevent systems from altering their own records or authorizing their own deployment. Chinese and American companies have already disclosed some information about their use of AI in research, which provides a limited foundation for more systematic reporting. Independent evaluations and tamper-resistant logs would make such disclosures more credible and comparable.

U.S. labs could build on what Chinese companies already do by publishing clearer, more detailed accounts of how they automate research. Chinese companies, in turn, could go beyond stating that humans remain in the loop and specify the safeguards actually in place to govern increasingly autonomous systems. Greater transparency about AI R&D automation would give researchers on both sides a concrete basis for engagement. This does not require unrestricted disclosure of sensitive research, or either side adopting the other’s standards wholesale. Converging on a common reporting baseline would support information exchange and help both sides assess emerging capabilities and risks without relying on vague claims or geopolitical speculation.
